Even so, evidence specific to this area remains fragmented, particularly with regard to the performance of individual AI frameworks, the way they have been validated, and their practical relevance to veterinary diagnostic anatomy. PURPOSE: This review critically examines current AI frameworks and models applied to diagnostic veterinary anatomy. Particular attention is given to how these approaches work, where they have been used, their reported diagnostic performance, their main strengths and limitations, the extent of validation, and areas that still require investigation. METHODS: Relevant studies were identified by searching PubMed and Scopus, and the retrieved literature was assessed to identify recent developments in AI-assisted diagnostic veterinary anatomy. After screening and eligibility assessment, 45 primary investigations were retained for the final synthesis. The review covers convolutional neural networks, Vision Transformer-based methods, segmentation frameworks, object-detection models, generative models, self-supervised learning approaches, and other AI techniques used for veterinary diagnostic and anatomical tasks. RESULTS: Across radiography, computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, ultrasonography, histopathology, and other anatomical imaging settings, several studies reported high internal performance for AI methods. The included investigations examined image classification, anatomical segmentation and localization, object detection, quantitative morphometry, disease detection, anatomical identification, and image enhancement. Nevertheless, the studies differed markedly in species, dataset size, design, performance measures, and validation strategy. Several models performed strongly on the datasets used for development, but independent external testing and prospective clinical evaluation were uncommon. CONCLUSIONS: Artificial intelligence has clear potential to support diagnostic veterinary anatomy in both research and clinical settings. Broader clinical use, however, will require larger and more representative datasets, consistent validation procedures, explainable methods, independent external assessment, and prospective clinical studies. Further progress in multimodal learning and clinically tested models may make AI more useful in veterinary anatomical diagnosis and precision veterinary medicine.
authors: Santosh Kumar Sahu; Uma Kanta Mishra

title: Artificial intelligence in early oral cancer detection: a comprehensive review of diagnostic applications, clinical implementation, and future directions
abstract: Oral cancer causes more than 377,000 new cases annually, and delayed diagnosis remains a major contributor to poor outcomes. Conventional visual examination is subjective, while specialist access is limited in many rural and resource-constrained settings.To review the diagnostic performance, clinical implementation, and future directions of artificial intelligence (AI) for early detection and risk stratification of oral potentially malignant disorders (OPMDs) and oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC).PubMed, Scopus, IEEE Xplore, and Web of Science were searched for English-language, peer-reviewed studies published from 2015 to 2026 using terms related to AI, machine learning, deep learning, OPMDs, OSCC, screening, and early detection. Eligible diagnostic and implementation studies were synthesized narratively because of methodological heterogeneity.Meta-analyses reported pooled sensitivities of 87%-92% and specificities of 81%-92% across mixed imaging and histopathology applications. PRAYAAS achieved 94% accuracy on its held-out test set, while OralCancerPredict showed good discrimination and calibration for malignant progression risk in oral leukoplakia. Nevertheless, most evidence remains retrospective, single-center, and vulnerable to dataset bias, limited external validation, and inconsistent reference standards.AI is a promising adjunct, not a replacement, for clinician-led screening and histopathologic diagnosis. Priorities include prospective multicenter validation, representative datasets, transparent reporting, explainability, workflow integration, cost-effectiveness, and equity-focused evaluation in low- and middle-income countries.
authors: Smit Kabrawala; Akshay Ashok Katara; Ikjyot Singh Gujral; Siddharth Jena

title: Shortages of Dental Personnel and Their Consequences for Healthcare
abstract: Introduction: The shortage of medical personnel remains one of the most acute problems in the domestic healthcare system; within dental services, this issue is particularly critical due to significant geographical and structural disparities in the distribution of specialists. Rising public demand for dental care—driven by demographic shifts and increased life expectancy—coincides with a declining influx of young specialists into primary care, a migration of personnel to the private sector, and uneven dentist staffing levels across regions. Official statistics indicate that the supply of dentists in a number of Russian regions falls short of established standards, directly impacting the accessibility and quality of care provided. This study is necessitated by the need for a systemic analysis of the factors driving this workforce imbalance and for the development of evidence-based management strategies to address it. Objectives: comprehensive assessment of the staffing situation in the dental service of the Russian Federation, identification of key factors contributing to the shortage, and development of scientifically grounded proposals to address it. Methods: A retrospective analysis was conducted using departmental data from the Russian Ministry of Health, Rosstat, and the Federal Compulsory Medical Insurance Fund (FOMS) for the period 2019–2025, covering indicators of the availability of dentists and dental practitioners, workforce structure, age distribution, and staff turnover. Regulatory acts governing healthcare workforce policy were examined. Comparative, statistical, and content analysis methods were employed. Results: It has been established that the average supply of dentists in the constituent entities of the Central Federal District is 3.1 per 10,000 population, against a benchmark of 4.0. The proportion of dentists of retirement age exceeds 28%. A positive correlation was identified between salary levels and the retention of young specialists. The primary factors contributing to the shortage were determined to be the lack of prestige associated with working in primary care, low motivation among graduates, and the underdeveloped state of targeted training programs. Conclusions: Addressing the shortage of dental personnel requires a comprehensive approach that includes improving targeted training mechanisms, modernizing incentive and motivation systems, advancing digital technologies in education and practice, and strengthening the role of primary care. Implementing these measures helps improve the accessibility and quality of dental care for the population.
authors: Пак Виталий Игоревич

title: Clinical Applications of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Dentistry: A Scoping Review
abstract: Introduction: The digital transition in dentistry is driven by the integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Large Language Models (LLMs). Objective: To map the efficacy, clinical applicability, and ethical-legal limitations of these technologies across various dental specialties through a scoping review. Methodology: A literature review based on seven review articles was conducted, analyzing the impact of various Generative AI models on diagnosis, treatment planning, patient communication, and oral health education. Results: Imaging AI achieves excellent levels of precision (>90%) in the diagnosis of carious lesions, periapical pathology, periodontology, and forensic identification. Medical robotics minimizes operative deviations in implantology. However, LLMs (e.g., ChatGPT) demonstrate heterogeneous results; although they reduce patient anxiety in clinical communication, they exhibit insufficient precision in prosthodontic and complex orthodontic planning, suffering from "hallucinations" and an inability for autonomous scientific validation. Conclusions: AI constitutes an exceptional adjunctive resource for precision dentistry. However, its implementation requires the mitigation of algorithmic biases, structured data protection, and the prevention of the impairment of critical thinking among professionals. Final validation and therapeutic responsibility must remain intrinsically linked to the dentist, in accordance with the human-in-the-loop model. Keywords: Dentistry; Generative Artificial Intelligence; Patient Communication; Treatment Planning; Diagnosis; Medical Ethics.
authors: Sara da Silva Antunes

title: Case Report: Giant adult rhabdomyoma of the parapharyngeal space: diagnostic and surgical pitfalls
abstract: Background Adult-type extracardiac rhabdomyoma is a rare benign skeletal-muscle neoplasm that most often arises in the head and neck but is exceptional in the parapharyngeal space, where it may mimic salivary or neurogenic tumours. Case presentation: A 67-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of progressive dysphagia, globus sensation, and mild hoarseness. Computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated an approximately 9-cm, well-circumscribed right parapharyngeal mass with relatively homogeneous internal characteristics and mild-to-moderate enhancement. Because direct glottic exposure was inadequate, tracheotomy-assisted airway management preceded complete excision through a right lateral transcervical approach. Histopathology showed large polygonal cells with abundant eosinophilic granular cytoplasm. The tumour was positive for desmin and smooth-muscle actin, with focal MyoD1 and myogenin expression, a low Ki-67 labelling index, and negative S-100 staining, supporting adult-type rhabdomyoma. Recovery was uneventful, and magnetic resonance imaging at 6 and 12 months showed no recurrence. Conclusion Adult rhabdomyoma should be considered in the differential diagnosis of a well-circumscribed parapharyngeal mass in an older adult. Integrated radiological and pathological assessment, careful airway planning, complete conservative excision, and long-term surveillance are central to management.
authors: Bingyi Dai; Hongyang Qu; Rong Liu; Changling Sun; Xiao Yin

title: Artificial intelligence application in dentistry: umbrella systematic review
abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) is a field of computer science that employs algorithms to simulate smart decisions made by humans. It has made significant advances in the dental field in recent years. Although several systematic reviews on the use of AI in dentistry have been conducted, no comprehensive analysis of the current state of AI development and performance in dental applications has been published. Purpose: This umbrella systematic review aims to explore the expanding role of AI systems in dentistry, focusing on their applications in diagnostics, clinical decision-making, and prognosis. These core domains are essential to dental care delivery, as they directly impact treatment accuracy, planning, and outcomes. By synthesizing current evidence, this review seeks to identify advances, reveal research gaps, and support the integration of AI into routine dental practice. Methods: This study was conducted pursuant to the PRISMA guidelines. A search for full-length articles used the terms “Artificial Intelligence,” “Dentistry,” “Application,” “Systematic,” and “Review.” Results: This systematic review included articles discussing dental and maxillofacial radiology, deep learning models, endodontics, periodontics, forensic odontology, dental implants, dental caries detection, cancer detection, conservative dentistry, prosthodontics, and high-quality patient care. AI models can be considered an assistant in diagnosis, treatment, and prognosis across these various dental fields. Conclusion: AI models have demonstrated potential abilities for diagnostic, therapeutic, and prognostic evaluations in dentistry. For their safe integration into routine clinical practice, it is critical to improve these models in terms of explainability, interpretability, and generalizability through external validation. Applying these models in clinical procedures entails the need to establish appropriate regulatory frameworks.
authors: Mona Abdulrahman Abdullah Al-Hadi; Suha Mudhish Abduljalil Ahmed; Syifa Salsabila Eddy; Afrida Nurmalasari; Kaushik Sengupta; Ninuk Hariyani

title: Artificial Intelligence in CBCT for Dental Implantology: Current Applications, Limitations, and Future Perspectives - A Literature Review
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being integrated into cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT)-based workflows in dental implantology.This structured narrative literature review evaluated current AI applications in implant dentistry, critically assessed their technical and clinical limitations, and discussed future perspectives for integration into implant planning and treatment workflows.A literature search was conducted using PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, and Embase.Evidence was synthesized according to clinically relevant domains, including anatomical segmentation, identification of edentulous regions and implant sites, bone assessment, virtual implant planning, comparison with expert planning, workflow optimization, and outcome prediction.AI demonstrated encouraging performance in CBCT segmentation, anatomical and bone assessment, and selected components of virtual implant planning.Automated systems showed substantial agreement with expert-generated plans in selected clinical settings and consistently reduced planning time while providing high repeatability.However, performance varied according to anatomical complexity, imaging conditions, software environment, and the specific task evaluated.Limited external validation, heterogeneous datasets and evaluation methods, and the gap between technical performance and demonstrated clinical benefit remain important barriers to generalizability.Current evidence supports AI primarily as a decision-support tool that complements professional judgment.Future research should prioritize multicenter prospective validation, standardized evaluation frameworks, multimodal data integration, explainable and uncertainty-aware models, and clinically meaningful outcomes.
authors: Nabil EL SAHILI
venue: Online Journal of Dentistry & Oral Health

title: ROBOTICS IN ENDODONTICS: AN INTEGRATIVE REVIEW OF AUTONOMY AND TRANSLATIONAL READINESS
abstract: Background: Existing syntheses of endodontic robotics import autonomy terminology from implant robotics, separate the macro- and micro-robotic literatures, and report performance without appraising the evidence. Methods: This integrative review searched PubMed to 31 July 2026, supplemented by Google Scholar and citation tracking, purposively selecting 61 records graded on the OCEBM 2011 hierarchy and assigned technology-readiness levels. No human participants or animals were involved; ethical approval was not applicable. Conclusion: The bottleneck is translational rather than conceptual.
authors: Prabhav Patel; Aabha Bhaskar Rawal; Zalak Patel

title: Artificial Intelligence in Invisible Orthodontics: From Digital Impressions to Adaptive Treatment Management
abstract: ABSTRACT Digital transformation in orthodontics has significantly revolutionized clinical practices over recent decades. Advancements such as intraoral scanners, 3D imaging (including cone‐beam computed tomography, CBCT), and advanced treatment planning software have increased diagnostic accuracy and the ability to design personalized treatments. These technologies have primarily focused on static aspects and still require continuous human oversight. Machine learning algorithms, particularly convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and artificial neural networks (ANNs), offer superior performance in tasks such as identifying anatomical landmarks on radiographic images, assessing skeletal maturity, and predicting treatment outcomes. Research has shown that AI in static diagnosis and planning has achieved an accuracy greater than 90%, outperforming traditional methods. Moreover, AI reduces processing time, minimizes operator performance variability, and serves as a supportive tool in digital orthodontic workflows. Despite these advancements, there remains a significant gap in research regarding adaptive AI for treatments involving clear aligners. Most studies focus on static planning, while dynamic aspects, such as real‐time treatment adjustments based on the patient's biological responses or deviations in tooth movement, are less explored. This research gap may arise from factors such as patient biological diversity, a lack of real clinical data, and the need for multi‐center validation. Adaptive AI, based on reinforcement learning and digital twin modeling, has the potential to reduce the average treatment duration by approximately 3 to 4 months and increase patient satisfaction. The aim of this review is to provide a comprehensive examination of AI's role in real‐time management of invisible orthodontic treatments, focusing on clear aligner‐based treatments. This study analyzes AI applications going from digital data processing to integration with supervisory platforms, discussing challenges, limitations, and future perspectives. This review not only summarizes current achievements but also proposes practical solutions to overcome existing barriers and presents adaptive AI as a pivotal tool for the future of orthodontics.
authors: Soodeh Hosseini; Hossein Seilani; At‐har Nasari

title: CAD/CAM Technologies, Three-Dimensional Printing, and Contemporary Dental Materials
abstract: CAD/CAM technologies have transformed the production of fixed prosthodontic restorations from a craft based on manual skill into a standardized and measurable digital process. This chapter addresses, for dental students in their clinical years and for early-career clinicians, the fundamental principles of CAD/CAM systems, digital and artificial intelligence-assisted restoration design, milling and three-dimensional printing technologies, contemporary restorative materials, the factors influencing material selection, accuracy and quality control in digital manufacturing, and the biocompatible and smart materials of the future, in the light of the current and verified literature. The digital workflow comprises three interdependent links—data acquisition, design, and manufacturing—and the quality of the final restoration is limited by the weakest link in the chain. Although milling remains the gold standard for definitive restorations, additive manufacturing has become established for interim restorations, models, and surgical guides, and it is a rapidly maturing alternative for definitive restorations. On the material side, the rise of monolithic zirconia, the diversification of lithium silicate glass-ceramics, and the establishment of resin-matrix ceramics in minimally invasive applications offer the clinician a broad range of options with varying levels of evidence. Current systematic-review and meta-analytic evidence shows that AI-assisted design shortens design time and improves reproducibility, but that human oversight remains indispensable. Clinical success depends on manufacturing the right material with validated parameters for the right indication and applying it with an appropriate adhesive or conventional cementation protocol. Accuracy should be defined by its trueness and precision components, marginal fit should be evaluated against clinical acceptability thresholds, and quality control should be maintained at every link of the digital chain. The graded, bioactive, self-healing, and stimuli-responsive materials of the future, together with additively manufactured ceramics, signal a transition from passive to smart materials in restorative dentistry.
authors: Muhammed Mustafa Akar; Alptuğ Kendirci

title: A Hybrid YOLO-NAS Technology in Transforming Autonomous Vehicle Manufacturing
abstract: Object detection, the core fundamental task of the environmental perception module for autonomous driving, still faces a bottleneck that is difficult to break through. Four types of interference, namely severe weather, low illumination, partial occlusion, and sensor noise, all reduce detection accuracy, which in turn weakens the reliability of core decision-making for safe driving. This study proposes a hybrid perception scheme based on YOLO-NAS that meets the indispensable requirement of real-time performance. By integrating the NAS-optimized architecture and connecting multi-step processing in sequence, the scheme improves the robustness of recognition in complex scenarios. The proposed framework was evaluated on the nuScenes autonomous driving benchmark using the official dataset split. Experimental evaluation under daytime, nighttime, and adverse weather conditions demonstrates that the proposed approach consistently achieves detection accuracies of 94–96%, outperforming YOLOv8 (84–89%) and YOLOv7 (79–81%). Overall, YOLO-NAS provides performance gains of approximately 5–10% over YOLOv8 and 13–25% over YOLOv7 while maintaining stable inference and improved robustness against partially occluded objects and challenging visual conditions. These results demonstrate that incorporating NAS into the YOLO detection pipeline improves perception reliability and detection consistency, offering a practical solution for enhancing the safety, robustness, and real-world deployment of autonomous vehicle perception systems.
authors: Adi El‐Dalahmeh; Layla Albdour; Mohammad Alia

title: Clinical readiness and generalizability of artificial intelligence in implant dentistry: a systematic review of diagnostic accuracy, treatment planning, prognosis and external validation
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being incorporated into digital dentistry. In implant dentistry, machine-learning and deep-learning systems have been investigated for radiographic diagnosis, anatomical segmentation, treatment planning, prosthetically driven implant positioning, and prediction of implant-related outcomes. To systematically evaluate the clinical applications of AI in implant dentistry, with particular emphasis on diagnostic accuracy, treatment planning, prognosis, external validation, generalizability, and clinical applicability. A systematic review will be conducted according to PRISMA 2020. PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, Embase, and Cochrane Library will be searched from inception to the final search date. Studies evaluating AI, machine learning, deep learning, neural networks, or related computational approaches in human implant dentistry will be considered. Diagnostic studies will be assessed using QUADAS-2, prognostic studies using QUAPAS where applicable, and prediction-model studies using PROBAST+AI. Reporting quality of prediction models will be assessed using TRIPOD+AI. Current evidence demonstrates promising AI performance in anatomical segmentation, CBCT analysis, implant treatment planning, prosthetically driven positioning, and prediction of implant-related outcomes. However, the literature is heterogeneous with respect to datasets, algorithms, reference standards, outcome definitions, validation procedures, and performance measures. Many studies remain retrospective, and external validation and evidence of clinical utility are comparatively limited. AI has considerable potential as a decision-support technology in implant dentistry. The principal research priority is now progression from technical accuracy toward externally validated, explainable, calibrated, clinically useful, and patient-centered AI systems. Keywords AI; machine learning; deep learning; dental implants; implant dentistry; CBCT; implant planning; implant prognosis; peri-implantitis; digital dentistry.
authors: Rohit Raghavan; P. A. Shajahan; Akash R.
venue: International Journal of Research in Medical Sciences

title: Tensions in Dental AI Systems Adoption: A Narrative Review of Challenges and Opportunities
abstract: Artificial intelligence-based systems (AIS) are becoming part of dentistry. Their integration raises unresolved tensions for users such as trust, explainability, responsibility, professional autonomy and real-world usefulness. This concise review examines these tensions and discusses how they may shape the adoption of AIS in dentistry. This concise review was designed as a narrative review. An initial screening suggested that challenges associated with the implementation of AIS in dentistry appear to remain insufficiently explored in the dental literature. An author with expertise in marketing then formulated a list of AIS implementation issues considered well established in marketing research, drawing particularly on reference publications from leading journals. Based on these issues, the authors identified a set of tensions, and the dental authors translated them into concrete examples and implications for dental implementation. In dentistry, these tensions arise at three interconnected levels. At the human level, AIS may support diagnosis, risk communication and shared decision-making, but may also foster over-reliance or unjustified rejection. At the human–AIS interface, tools can flag lesions, prioritise cases or automate workflows that redistribute agency and require clear boundaries between assistance, delegation and responsibility. At the AIS level, dental applications face persistent issues of generalisability, privacy, adaptability and validation across populations, devices and care settings. The value of AIS in dentistry will depend less on technical performance alone than on the capacity to design, evaluate and implement user-centered tools with a co-designed approach involving all stakeholders, from patients and clinicians to institutions and decision-makers. Anticipating these tensions may help support trustworthy, context-sensitive and sustainable AIS adoption in oral health care.
authors: Maxime Ducret; Falk Schwendicke; Julien Cloarec

title: Orofacial pain disorder or trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia? Insights into pathophysiology and implications in medicine and dentistry
abstract: OBJECTIVE: This narrative review highlights the importance of orofacial pain considerations in the differential diagnosis of trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias (TACs)/trigeminal autonomic orofacial pains (TAOPs). In addition, we provide novel insights into the pathophysiology of the presentation of TACs in the maxillary (V2) and mandibular (V3) trigeminal distributions (TAOPs). BACKGROUND: TACs are lifelong disorders characterized by severe unilateral head pain accompanied by cranial autonomic phenomena. However, the head pain experienced may refer to the face, be present solely in the orofacial region as TAOPs, or even be experienced as a toothache. These presentations, involving V2/V3, may resemble disorders of diverse etiology and pathophysiology that may share some similarities with TACs, confusing the patient while relating symptoms, and creating a diagnostic dilemma for the clinician potentially leading to misdiagnosis. Moreover, TACs pathophysiology has not been discussed in relation to V2/V3 presentations (TAOPs). METHODS: A literature search was performed on PubMed/Scopus to find relevant literature about TACs and TAOPs, and case reports of orofacial presentations. Deep reanalysis of several of our published articles on preclinical models of TACs was conducted to assess potential of V2-V3 components. RESULTS: TACs orofacial presentations are not as common but if present can lead to misdiagnosis with significant consequences. Patients presenting TACs involving the midface as TAOPs experience an important delay for a correct diagnosis including multiple and diverse health provider visits, with a risk of having well-intended but misguided procedures. Differential diagnosis considerations need to include dental/odontogenic causes, sinusitis, temporomandibular disorders, Eagle syndrome, trigeminal neuralgia, and migraine (orofacial migraine, neurovascular orofacial pain). A reanalysis of preclinical data provides novel insights into this orofacial involvement. In two TAC-specific preclinical neuronal populations, recording either trigeminal or superior salivatory nucleus neurons, it was observed that ~20% and 37.5% of neurons, respectively, had cutaneous receptive fields that included or were exclusively within the V2-V3 trigeminal division. Whereas the numbers are not large, these demonstrate that even in rodent models in neuronal populations that could be considered TAC-like, they can extend to, or exclusively involve, the facial region, similar to TAOPs. CONCLUSION: The potential presence of TACs in the orofacial region can be observed from preclinical models to the clinical setting. The International Classification of Headache Disorders (ICHD) needs to recognize this additional localization, as well as the intraoral one, including dental structures. Education about TACs/TAOPs in the medical and dental setting is vital. Evidence has shown that dentists are one of the first providers that are seen by this patient population due to similarities with dental pain. The dentist specialized in orofacial pain is a key ally in the identification of TACs/TAOPs. The medical/neurology and dental/orofacial pain settings have a great opportunity and responsibility to work together to stop years of pain in this patient population.

title: Artificial Intelligence Systems in Prosthodontics: Current Applications and Challenges
abstract: BACKGROUND: The rapid development of artificial intelligence systems (AIS) in prosthodontics requires an overview of their applications, capabilities, opportunities and challenges. METHODS: This narrative review provides insights into AIS in prosthodontics and their applications. AI systems were classified into five main categories: (1) automated image handling and annotation; (2) classification and decision support; (3) visualisation and modelling; (4) optimisation and simulation; and (5) recording and communication. RESULTS: These AIS in prosthodontics can be used to delineate restorative margins in computer-aided design and manufacturing workflows, digital restoration design to generate crown proposals from intraoral scanning data, or conversational interfaces to provide clear, accessible and personalised explanations to patients. These systems offer significant capabilities, such as in diagnostic and treatment planning support, optimisation of prosthetic design, improved efficiency of digital workflows and enhanced patient communication. However, important challenges must be considered including the risk of automation bias, the lack of system transparency and explainability, issues related to equity and data protection and the ethical and medico-legal uncertainties surrounding accountability in the event of treatment failure. CONCLUSIONS: These systems offer significant capabilities in prosthodontics, but important challenges must be considered.
authors: Marjorie Faure; Catherine Millet; Raphaël Richert; Rata Rokhshad; Faleh Tamimi; Maxime Ducret

title: Pilot comparison of nine large language models generating radiological reports from dental panoramic radiograph pathology notation
abstract: Abstract Large language models (LLMs) may help convert structured pathology notations derived from dental panoramic radiographs (DPRs) into radiological reports, but comparative data remain limited. This pilot head-to-head study evaluated nine publicly available LLMs across five domains: correct tooth numbering, correct diagnosis assignment, avoidance of confabulations, proper radiological terminology, and avoidance of repetitions. Nineteen anonymized DPRs from an open-source repository were converted into standardized pathology notations by an experienced clinician. Nine LLMs generated reports from identical prompts and identical input data without task-specific fine-tuning. Report quality was rated on a 3-point ordinal scale. Between-model differences were assessed using the Friedman test with Nemenyi post-hoc comparisons; accuracy and F1-scores were also calculated. Significant between-model differences were found in correct diagnosis assignment, avoidance of confabulations, and proper radiological terminology, whereas differences were smaller in correct tooth numbering and avoidance of repetitions. The strongest overall performance was achieved by o1 and o3-mini (accuracy: 0.91 and 0.92; F1-score: 0.95 and 0.96), with o3-mini-high also performing strongly (accuracy: 0.87; F1-score: 0.93). No model consistently met expert expectations across all domains. Performance differed significantly between models. Reasoning-oriented models, particularly o1 and o3-mini, performed best overall, especially in correct diagnosis assignment and avoidance of confabulations. LLM-assisted radiological reporting appears promising, but current performance does not support autonomous clinical use and still requires expert oversight. Moreover, the findings reflect model versions available at the time of testing and should not be interpreted as a definitive ranking of LLM performance.
authors: Kamila Chęcińska; Maciej Adam Chęciński; Natalia Turosz; Bartosz Bartoszewski; Amelia Hoppe; Harish Tayyar Madabushi; Paolo Iacoviello; Maciej Sikora

title: Duagnosis: Locating Clinical Uncertainty in the Diagnostic Framework
abstract: RATIONALE, AIMS AND OBJECTIVES: Clinical reasoning research has predominantly operated within a single epistemological system. The prevailing response to clinical uncertainty in primary care has been to cultivate tolerance, embrace ambiguity, or learn to navigate it: each treats uncertainty as inherent to the encounter. We propose a complementary move. Much of what is called clinical uncertainty may be attributed less to the patient's condition than to the reach of the diagnostic framework through which the clinician reasons. We introduce the concept of duagnosis (dual + gnosis, 'knowing'): the clinical cognition in which two independent diagnostic systems are simultaneously activated within a single clinician's reasoning. METHODS: Conceptual analysis proceeding through concept definition, differentiation from neighbouring frameworks, development of the epistemological argument, and institutional comparison across East Asia. The analysis draws on clinical reasoning research, the philosophy of medicine, evidence on the care of persistent physical symptoms, and comparative scholarship on traditional medicine. RESULTS: The core contribution is epistemological: what one framework cannot formulate may resolve into a recognisable, actionable pattern in another, so that uncertainty is partly a property of the framework and not only of the patient. Duagnosis can be stated in two versions: a broad sense continuous with family medicine's plural readings of the patient, and a strict sense in which the criteria of evidence themselves change. An East Asian institutional comparison shows that Japan's unified medical licence locates diagnostic duality within individual clinician cognition for every physician, a capacity medical education has not cultivated. CONCLUSION: Expanding the diagnostic repertoire, not merely tolerating uncertainty, can reduce the proportion of presentations for which no clinical formulation exists. Locating uncertainty partly in the reach of the framework, rather than in the patient, is a reframing that applies beyond any one health system, with implications for communication and referral.
authors: Kosei HANAOKA; Daisuke Miyamori; Keiko Ogawa‐Ochiai

title: The perceived facilitators and barriers to the potential adoption of teledentistry among dental care providers in Saudi Arabia: A systematic review
abstract: Teledentistry has emerged as a tool that holds great potential to enhance access, efficiency, and continuity of oral healthcare delivery. In Saudi Arabia, its adoption is important in the context of the health transformation programme and Vision 2030, particularly given the high prevalence of dental caries among schoolchildren. Despite this potential, actual implementation is still limited. In this context, there is a need to systematically assess the factors influencing its potential adoption from the care providers' perspectives. This review aimed to systematically identify how dental care providers perceive the facilitators and barriers to the adoption of teledentistry in Saudi Arabia, with a focus on the perception of dental care providers, including dental students. Following PRISMA 2020 and SWiM guidelines, PubMed, Scopus, Medline, Embase, and CINAHL databases were searched, covering publications up to 4 July 2025. The PICO framework was used to define the inclusion and exclusion criteria, and the CASP checklist was used to assess study quality. Data were synthesised using vote counting by direction of effect, categorising findings into facilitators and barriers. Out of 156 records, 11 studies met the inclusion criteria. Study quality ranged from 7 to11 out of 11 based on the CASP checklist for cross-sectional studies. Key findings included potential facilitators such as improved access, efficiency and cost-effectiveness, communication and referral enhancements, educational benefits, and positive perception of technology. The key reported barriers were limited awareness and training, infrastructure and equipment reliability, privacy and data security, cost and financial issues, diagnostic accuracy, and the preference for in-person meetings. While teledentistry holds great potential, its integration in Saudi Arabia could be hindered by educational and technical challenges. Addressing them through improved infrastructure, enhanced training and integration into dental curricula, and strengthened regulatory frameworks may facilitate and support equitable adoption.
authors: Amjad Hakami; Sarika Mohan

title: Comparative life cycle assessment of traditional and computer-guided dental surgical procedures
abstract: Purpose In recent years, dental implantology has greatly benefited from the introduction of innovative techniques aimed at improving clinical outcomes, reducing healing time and increasing patient comfort. However, the environmental implications of digital techniques remain unexplored. The purpose of this study is to assess and compare the environmental sustainability of traditional and digital dental implant placement workflows. Design/methodology/approach This study presents a comparative life cycle assessment (LCA) of two dental implant placement workflows: traditional technique and computer-guided approach. The latter exploits a 3D scanner and 3D printing technology to produce a surgical guide for implant placement. The analysis followed the ISO14040-44 standards and was conducted using data collected in a clinical environment and secondary data from literature and Ecoinvent database. The functional unit was defined as the surgical workflow for placing four implants, and impacts from preoperative, operative and postoperative phases were included. Findings Results showed that the computer-guided procedure reduced the global warming potential by 17% compared with the traditional approach (from 8.53 to 7.05 kg CO2 eq), mainly due to lower energy use and the elimination of consumable materials such as impression trays and plaster. The environmental contribution of digital technology machines was almost negligible due to low energy consumption and efficient material use. Results reliability was confirmed via a sensitivity analysis. Originality/value To the best of the authors’ knowledge, this study provides the first comprehensive LCA of traditional and computer-guided dental implant workflows, demonstrating that digitalization and additive manufacturing can significantly improve the environmental sustainability of the dental healthcare sector.
authors: Iacopo Bianchi; Eleonora Claudia Casamassima; Archimede Forcellese; Francesco Valente; Tonino Traini

title: AI Rickshaw: A Secure, Geofenced, Solar-Assisted Autonomous Electric Rickshaw for Bangladesh and the Displacement Risk to the Lowest-Income Transport Workers
abstract: Bangladesh moves on rickshaws: a quarter of Dhaka's trips are made by cycle or battery-assisted rickshaw, and one to two million battery-run three-wheelers in the capital each support a driver from one of Bangladesh's lowest-income informal transport workforces. This article presents AI Rickshaw, a reference design for a driverless, app-summoned, solar-assisted electric rickshaw (AIR-1) that keeps the traditional three-wheel form, and uses it as a Bangladesh-specific case study in embodied artificial intelligence. Four contributions are made. First, a reference architecture adapted to lane-less, low-speed, high-density traffic. Second, software-enforced traffic compliance: geofenced operation in which highways, restricted roads, wrong-way movement and out-of-zone trips cannot be planned or executed, so that regulation becomes executable rather than merely instructive. Third, an integrated cyber-physical security architecture for theft, tampering, unauthorised control and passenger emergencies, in which a hard-wired safety microcontroller is the sole validated actuator gateway, so that compromise of the back end does not directly confer actuator authority. Fourth, an argument, with scenario evidence, that embodied AI, the combination of perception, robotics, electric actuation and digital platforms, can threaten the lowest-income manual occupations and not only knowledge work: under the base adoption scenario, substantial displacement of Dhaka's drivers could occur by 2041, and a just-transition framework of a per-vehicle-day levy, garage franchising, microfinance co-ownership and evidence-gated deployment is proposed. Solar energy is treated as assisting, not primary, supply. No physical prototype has yet been built; every quantitative value carries its evidence type, and the next phase is a hardware prototype validated in a private geofenced environment.
authors: Md Israfeel

title: Development and internal validation of a deep learning system for criterion-specific assessment of preclinical dental soap carvings: a multi-rater study
abstract: Preclinical dental morphology education, assessment of soap-carving exercises may be influenced by inter-rater variability and the workload associated with manual evaluation. This study developed and internally evaluated an artificial intelligence (AI)–based deep learning system for criterion-specific assessment of soap carvings and examined its agreement with an averaged multi-rater reference standard. A total of 280 soap-carved maxillary left permanent central incisors (Fédération Dentaire Internationale [FDI] tooth 21) were photographed in five standardized views (1,400 images). Three educators independently scored each specimen on ten morphological criteria using a 0–10 scale. Inter-rater reliability was assessed using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs), and mean ratings formed criterion-specific averaged multi-rater reference scores. Specimens were partitioned into a development set ( n = 224) and an internal hold-out test set ( n = 56). A ResNet50-based multi-output regression model was trained using five-fold cross-validation across three random seeds and two-stage transfer learning. Performance was evaluated using mean absolute error (MAE), root mean squared error (RMSE), coefficient of determination (R²), Spearman’s rank correlation, ICC, Bland–Altman analysis, and bootstrap 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) was qualitatively examined in eight hold-out specimens. Average-measure ICCs among educators ranged from 0.849 to 0.994 across the ten criteria. On the hold-out test set, the ensemble achieved a macro MAE of 1.204 (95% CI, 1.059–1.374), macro RMSE of 1.584 (95% CI, 1.371–1.799), and macro R² of 0.223 (95% CI, 0.023–0.348). Criterion-specific Spearman correlations ranged from 0.297 to 0.560, while absolute-agreement ICCs between AI predictions and averaged multi-rater reference scores ranged from 0.309 to 0.429. Criterion 10 had the lowest MAE (0.709), whereas Criterion 9 had the highest (2.029). Bland–Altman mean biases were small, with variable limits of agreement. Grad-CAM showed heterogeneous activation patterns. The findings demonstrate the feasibility of a ResNet50-based approach for criterion-specific assessment of soap carvings, while highlighting substantial variability in criterion-level performance. Absolute agreement with the multi-rater reference standard was heterogeneous and does not support interchangeability with educators assessment or autonomous summative grading. The approach may support human-supervised formative assessment, though prospective external validation is required before implementation.
authors: Göknur ÖZTÜRK; Özlem Kara; Hasan Efe Purmut; Mehmet Berk Birdal; Aysun Sezer

title: Dental Anxiety in Children: A Review on Etiology, Prevalence, and Assessment Methods
abstract: Dental anxiety is a common psychological problem in pediatric dentistry and remains a major obstacle to successful treatment. Although various behavioral techniques and technological advancements have been introduced, many children still exhibit anxiety during dental procedures, leading to treatment avoidance, poorer oral health, and reduced cooperation. The etiology of dental anxiety is multifactorial, shaped by individual traits, family influences, and past dental experiences. Early and accurate assessment of anxiety levels is essential for guiding clinical decisions and selecting appropriate management strategies. Effective anxiety control enhances cooperation during treatment and helps establish positive attitudes toward oral care. This review summarizes the main causes of pediatric dental anxiety, commonly used assessment tools, and current evidence-based approaches for its management, emphasizing the importance of early intervention for improved clinical outcomes.
authors: Büşra Almas

title: Performance and Hallucination Analysis of Large Language Models on European Anesthesiology Examinations: Cross-Sectional Comparative Study
abstract: Abstract Background Large language models (LLMs) have shown promising performance on medical examinations across specialties. However, comparative evaluations of current-generation LLMs across multiple European anesthesiology examinations, alongside structured assessment of hallucinations vs question-related confusion, remain lacking. Objective This study aimed to compare the performance of 4 state-of-the-art LLMs on anesthesiology and intensive medicine examination questions and assess their hallucination rates. Methods This computational comparative study analyzed 437 multiple-choice questions (1748 queries) from 3 sources: nurse anesthetist school examinations (infirmier anesthésiste diplômé d’État [registered nurse anesthetist]; n=100, 22.9%), European Diploma in Anaesthesiology and Intensive Care (EDAIC; n=219, 50.1%), and EDAIC On-Line Assessment (n=118, 27.0%). Each question was submitted to 4 LLMs (Claude Sonnet 4.5, Gemini 2.5 Pro, GPT-5, and Grok 4) using standardized prompts via default web interface settings. Responses were evaluated through structured consensus review by 2 examiners for accuracy, hallucinations, and question-related confusion. Statistical analysis included Friedman and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Holm-Bonferroni correction, the Cochran Q test, and generalized estimating equations. Results Average success rates ranged from 86% (SD 18%) to 94% (SD 10%) across LLMs and examination types, exceeding the EDAIC part I passing threshold, representing substantial improvement over previously reported GPT-3.5 performance. For the EDAIC, overall intermodel differences were significant (Friedman χ 2 3 =13.9; P =.003; W =0.02), with Gemini outperforming GPT-5 as the only pairwise difference. Hallucination rates ranged from 11% (11/100) to 20.1% (44/219) without significant intermodel differences. All models exceeded the EDAIC passing threshold. Conclusions Current-generation LLMs demonstrated consistently high performance across multiple European anesthesiology examinations but continue to produce clinically relevant hallucinations, supporting their role as supervised educational tools rather than autonomous learning resources. These findings underscore the need for structured integration frameworks and systematic verification when deploying LLMs as learning tools in medical education.

title: Artificial Intelligence and Digital Impressions: The Positives and the Pitfalls
abstract: Digital impressions are now central to contemporary dental workflows, driven by advances in CAD/CAM manufacturing and intraoral scanning technologies. In parallel, rapid progress in artificial intelligence (AI)-particularly deep learning-has led to its widespread integration into digital impression systems. AI already provides tangible clinical benefits, including real-time artefact removal, improved scan stitching, and more efficient three-dimensional data acquisition. However, these same techniques introduce new risks, most notably the silent modification or completion of scan data in regions of low confidence. Such inferred geometry may appear anatomically plausible while no longer representing a faithful record of the patient. This article examines where AI currently enhances digital impression accuracy and efficiency, and where it may compromise clinical validity. By distinguishing between beneficial data filtering and potentially misleading data inference, the aim is to support clinicians in making informed decisions and maintaining appropriate scrutiny of AI-assisted digital impressions.
authors: Andrew J. Keeling

title: Tribology of dental materials: from laboratory metrics to clinical durability: review and translational roadmap
abstract: The functional integrity of dental restorations is known by their resilience within the dynamic and hostile tribological ecosystem of the oral cavity. Despite significant advancements in material science, the premature failure of restorations due to wear remains a critical clinical challenge, rooted in a persistent disconnect between controlled laboratory metrics and unpredictable clinical realities. This review provides a comprehensive critical appraisal of dental tribology, delineating the complex interplay of wear mechanisms, attrition, abrasion, erosion, and abfraction, and evaluating the spectrum of current assessment methodologies, from fundamental in vitro simulations to advanced clinical quantification. We identified the primary limitations hindering accurate material prediction, specifically the lack of protocol standardization, the inability to replicate synergistic degradation processes such as tribo-corrosion, and the exclusion of patient-specific variables. To bridge this translational gap, we proposed a strategic roadmap integrating multi-tiered testing standardization, finite element analysis, and machine learning to enhance predictive capabilities. Furthermore, we advocated for the development of clinically relevant in vitro models that incorporate patient-specific parameters, such as occlusal loading profiles and salivary properties. By shifting the paradigm from descriptive testing to predictive, patient-centric material science, this review outlined a transformative pathway for the development of next-generation restorative materials, ultimately optimizing clinical longevity and treatment outcomes.
authors: Naif H. Al-Qahtani; Shahad Alqahtani; Shorooq K. Almajhad; Amjaad Almarzoogi; Noha Taymour

title: Development of software for use of dental mannequins in virtual environments or virtual reality and the metaverse
abstract: This research aims to present an interactive tool called OdontoSim 3D, which simulates dental procedures, providing an immersive educational experience, allowing risk-free practice for patients, and improving clinical skills. The use of detailed 3D models and features such as zoom and rotation enabled accurate analysis. The virtual system offers advantages over the use of physical mannequins, such as the elimination of clinical risks and cost reduction. The repetition of procedures and real-time interaction with three-dimensional models improved student learning. The software also showed scalability, allowing expansion to more complex procedures.
authors: Raissa Costa Silva; Nadja Maria da Silva Oliveira; Marcelo da Costa Borba

title: An Efficient Out-of-Core Tomographic Imaging Framework for Edge Devices
abstract: Computed Tomography (CT) is an essential 3D imaging technology widely used in medical diagnostics and scientific research. However, performing CT imaging on edge devices is challenging due to limitations in computational power, memory capacity, and energy budget. This paper presents an efficient CT reconstruction framework, called edgeFBP, designed for Nvidia Jetson System-on-Chip (SoC) devices. edgeFBP adopts an end-to-end pipeline design for efficient out-of-core image reconstruction under tight power and memory constraints. edgeFBP utilizes a mixed-precision strategy leveraging half-precision Tensor Cores (TCs) to accelerate the bottleneck back-projection (BP) kernel. edgeFBP achieves a 1.83x speedup over the widely used RTK library on Jetson Nano and a 2.56x speedup on Jetson AGX. Under a strict 25-Watt power budget, edgeFBP on Jetson Nano achieves up to 5-48x higher energy efficiency than an Nvidia DGX A100, enabling datacenter-scale imaging on constrained edge devices.
authors: Xuetao Chen; Cong Ma; Xiangyu Meng; Du Wu; Zhengyang Bai; Tao Luo; Zhaorui Zhang; Emmanuel Jeannot; Edgar Josafat Martinez Noriega; Xun Wang; Peng Chen; Amelie Chi Zhou; Mohamed Wahib

title: Biodigital Transformation in Dentistry: From Diagnosis and Biological Preservation to Multidisciplinary Rehabilitation
abstract: Advances in digital technologies have expanded diagnostic and treatment possibilities in dentistry while making the preservation of biological tissues and collaboration among specialties increasingly important. This book, *Biodigital Transformation in Dentistry: From Diagnosis and Biological Preservation to Multidisciplinary Rehabilitation*, was prepared to address these developments from an integrated perspective. It follows a scientific progression from biodigital diagnosis and clinical decision-making to preventive care in pediatric dentistry; from the preservation of the pulp and natural dentition to periodontal and orthodontic treatment; and from digital prosthetic planning to implant-supported rehabilitation. Written by contributors from different dental specialties, the chapters examine both the clinical applications and the limitations of current technologies. We hope this book will serve as a valuable resource for dental students, residents, academics, and clinicians, and we thank all the authors for their knowledge, time, and contributions.
