title: Diagnostic Accuracy of Multimodal Large Language Models for Four-Class Benchmark of Oral Autoimmune Blistering Diseases: A Multicenter Paired Study
abstract: Background/Objectives: To compare the diagnostic performance of Claude Opus 4.7 and Gemini Pro 3 for the differential diagnosis of oral autoimmune blistering diseases (AIBDs) and evaluate their diagnostic reasoning, confidence, and calibration. Materials and Methods: This retrospective multicenter paired diagnostic accuracy study included 200 clinicopathologically confirmed AIBD cases (50 each of pemphigus vulgaris, mucous membrane pemphigoid, bullous pemphigoid, and linear IgA bullous dermatosis). Each case was independently assessed by both models using identical standardized clinical information and clinical photographic inputs. The task required forced-choice classification among the four predefined diseases. Histopathological and direct immunofluorescence findings were used exclusively to establish the clinicopathological reference diagnosis and were not provided to the AI models. The reference diagnosis was established by clinicopathological correlation. The primary outcome was diagnostic accuracy. Secondary outcomes included disease-specific diagnostic performance, Cohen’s κ, ROC analysis, calibration, confidence, reasoning quality, management recommendations, and error patterns. Pre-consensus inter-rater reliability of the two human assessors was also evaluated using Cohen’s κ for binary outcomes and weighted Cohen’s κ for the ordinal reasoning-quality score. Results: Claude achieved significantly higher diagnostic accuracy than Gemini (92.0% vs. 86.0%, p = 0.012), stronger agreement with the reference standard (κ = 0.893 vs. 0.813), and superior discrimination (macro-AUC 0.998 vs. 0.965). Claude demonstrated higher key diagnostic-feature identification (92.0% vs. 86.0%; p = 0.012) and higher clinical-reasoning scores (61.0% vs. 40.0% of responses rated good; Wilcoxon p < 0.001; r = 0.47), whereas management recommendations did not differ significantly (100.0% vs. 98.0%; p = 0.125). Calibration results were metric-dependent: Claude had a lower one-vs-rest Brier score (0.0468 vs. 0.0558), whereas Gemini had a lower expected calibration error (0.083 vs. 0.251). For both models, the predominant error was misclassification of linear IgA bullous dermatosis as mucous membrane pemphigoid. Conclusions: Both multimodal LLMs showed high performance in this controlled four-class benchmark, with Claude Opus 4.7 outperforming Gemini Pro 3 in overall accuracy and reasoning quality. However, these findings do not establish autonomous diagnostic capability, clinical effectiveness, or safety. The LABD–MMP misclassification and metric-dependent calibration highlight important limitations. The models should therefore be regarded as investigational adjunctive decision-support tools requiring clinician oversight and diagnostic verification. Prospective external and human-in-the-loop validation is required before clinical implementation.
authors: Asmaa Abou‐Bakr; Salma M. Saad; Nevine H. Kheir El Din; Abdullah Bin Nabhan; Amal Bajonaid; Asma Almeslet; Fatma E. A. Hassanein

title: Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Quadrant-Level Treatment-Site Estimation for Patient Safety
abstract: Introduction and aims Safety interventions in dentistry, including checklists, have been reported; however, it remains difficult to demonstrate sufficient effectiveness in preventing treatment site misidentification, including wrong tooth extraction. This study aimed to establish a foundation for an artificial intelligence (AI)-based patient-safety measure by developing a system that estimates the dental treatment site at the quadrant level from images captured during dental procedures. Methods Single-frame still images (n = 2,446; training 1,780, validation 445, test 221) were extracted from clinical videos recorded during treatment performed by a single dentist between 27 July 2022 and 21 December 2023. Treatment-site estimation models were developed using VGG16, a convolutional neural network-based image-classification model, and YOLOv9, an object-detection model. Performance was compared using three metrics: quadrant accuracy (correct upper/lower and left/right), vertical accuracy (correct upper/lower only), and lateral accuracy (correct left/right only). Results Among five approaches (four VGG16 conditions and one YOLOv9 condition), YOLOv9 achieved the highest performance across all metrics, with quadrant accuracy of 88.7%, vertical accuracy of 96.8%, and lateral accuracy of 91.9%. For VGG16-based approaches, performance across these metrics varied according to image pre-processing. Conclusion This system may support detection and prevention of quadrant-level errors, which are reported to be the second most common type of wrong tooth extraction following adjacent-tooth errors. Clinical relevance AI-based treatment-site estimation may provide an additional preventive safety layer in dentistry by supporting clinicians’ judgement and enabling detection of quadrant-level site misidentification during dental procedures.
authors: Shintaro Nishimoto; Shintaro Oka; Kazunori Nozaki; Harumi Kitamura; Kyota Nakamura; Kazue Nakajima; Mikako Hayashi

title: Transoral Robotic Surgery in the Treatment of Head and Neck Cancer: Application and Prospect
abstract: Transoral robotic surgery (TORS) has reshaped the surgical management of head and neck neoplasms since its introduction in the mid-2000s, offering a minimally invasive transoral route to lesions of the oropharynx, larynx, hypopharynx, and nasopharynx. This narrative review synthesizes the technical foundations, current clinical evidence, and emerging directions of TORS, with explicit attention to study rigor and evidentiary hierarchy. Powered by the da Vinci platform, TORS provides magnified three-dimensional visualization and wristed instrumentation that enable en bloc resection with reduced external morbidity, shorter hospitalization, and the potential to spare or de-intensify adjuvant radiotherapy in selected human papillomavirus (HPV)-driven oropharyngeal cancers. For early-stage oropharyngeal disease, local control rates of 90–95% and disease-specific survival above 90% are consistently reported, and recent systematic reviews and large multicenter cohorts, including the international Recurrent Tumors of the Upper Aerodigestive Tract (RECUT) experience, confirm durable oncologic and functional outcomes in both primary and salvage settings, although randomized trials have yielded nuanced, sometimes divergent quality-of-life results. We appraise outcomes by anatomical subsite, the de-escalation trial landscape, complications and their mitigation, learning-curve dynamics, health economics, and the rapidly evolving integration of artificial intelligence in segmentation, augmented-reality navigation, intraoperative margin assessment, and outcome prediction. Recent evidence confirms that TORS is a valuable but expertise-dependent option whose benefit is greatest in carefully selected patients managed within multidisciplinary, high-volume pathways. We conclude by defining the principal unresolved questions and the evidence required to position TORS appropriately within contemporary multidisciplinary care.
authors: Qiang Huang; Chi‐Yao Hsueh; Jian Biao Zhou; Chengzhi Xu; Lei Tao

title: Role of Generative AI in Personalized Smile Design: A Clinical Evaluation of Esthetic Outcomes
abstract: Background Digital Smile Design (DSD) has become an important component of contemporary esthetic dentistry because it permits visualization of proposed dental changes before irreversible treatment. Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) may further enhance this process by rapidly producing individualized smile simulations. However, the esthetic value of AI-generated designs compared with conventional clinician-designed and clinician-refined designs remains incompletely established. Aim To evaluate the esthetic acceptability of generative-AI-assisted personalized smile designs and compare conventional Digital Smile Design, AI-generated smile design, and clinician-refined AI-assisted smile design. Materials and Methods A prospective comparative study was designed involving 60 adult participants seeking esthetic dental treatment. Standardized facial and intraoral photographs were obtained. Three smile-design conditions were produced: conventional clinician-generated DSD, AI-generated DSD, and AI-generated DSD subsequently refined by an experienced clinician. Patients and dental professionals independently evaluated the designs using a 10-point visual analogue scale (VAS), satisfaction assessment, and paired-preference testing. Objective digital parameters and design-generation time were also recorded. Repeated-measures data were analyzed using the Friedman test with pairwise comparisons. Results Illustrative simulated results: Mean patient VAS scores were 7.39 ± 0.64 for conventional DSD, 7.74 ± 0.76 for AI-generated DSD, and 8.37 ± 0.71 for AI-refined DSD. The overall difference was statistically significant (Friedman test, P < 0.001). Professional ratings were 7.89 ± 0.68, 7.35 ± 0.77, and 8.64 ± 0.76, respectively (P < 0.001). Mean design times were 62.4 ± 11.6, 24.8 ± 6.4, and 35.6 ± 7.8 minutes, respectively. Conclusion The illustrative findings suggest that generative AI may improve smile-design efficiency, while clinician refinement may further improve esthetic acceptance. The findings support an AI-assisted rather than AI-replacement model of personalized smile design. Actual patient data must replace the simulated dataset before scientific submission.
authors: Anand Awadhesh Tripathi; Anandadevi Chinnasamy; Dr. Vritti Aggarwal; Dr. Sunny Sharma; Dr. Nalumino Sayela; Imran Iqbal Patel

title: Limitations of off-the-shelf multimodal foundation models in secondary caries detection on interproximal radiographs
abstract: To evaluate whether off-the-shelf general-purpose multimodal foundation models can achieve clinically meaningful diagnostic performance in detecting secondary caries on interproximal radiographs without domain-specific training, using GPT-5o (OpenAI) and Gemini 2.5 Flash (Google Inc.) as representative publicly accessible models. A comparative exploratory study used 50 interproximal radiographs of posterior teeth obtained from a dental imaging center, yielding 208 teeth. Each tooth was evaluated twice by each model in independent sessions, totaling 416 observations per model. A specialist in restorative dentistry established the reference standard. Models were assessed in a zero-shot setting using a standardized prompt. Diagnostic performance was evaluated at the tooth level using accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, precision, F1-score, and Cohen's kappa, with 95% confidence intervals estimated via bootstrap resampling (1000 iterations). Both models demonstrated limited diagnostic performance. GPT-5o showed moderate sensitivity (64.7%) but low specificity (32.3%), resulting in an accuracy of 41.3% and negligible agreement with the reference standard (κ = - 0.021). Gemini 2.5 Flash exhibited higher sensitivity (82.8%) but extremely low specificity (13.0%), with lower accuracy (32.5%) and similarly negligible agreement (κ = - 0.026). Both models showed a strong tendency toward false-positive classifications. Tooth localization performance was poor, with low identification rates in both models. GPT-5o and Gemini 2.5 Flash, when used in their off-the-shelf configurations, demonstrated inadequate diagnostic performance for detecting secondary caries on interproximal radiographs. Their limited accuracy, low specificity, and poor localization ability do not support their direct use for secondary caries detection on interproximal radiographs without domain-specific training and rigorous independent validation.
authors: Camila Guimarães da Costa Campos; Cristiano Miranda de Araújo; Luana Beatriz das Portas Luiz; Diulia Pereira Bubna; Ângela Graciela Deliga Schröder; Flares Baratto‐Filho; Camila Paiva Perin; Bianca Marques de Mattos de Araujo; Thalita de Paris Matos

title: A Multimodal Autonomic Sensing Framework for Objective Assessment of Patient Responses to Dental Pulp Stimulation
abstract: Patient responses to dental pulp testing, ranging from no sensation to intense pain, provide important information for assessing pulp status in endodontic diagnosis. However, pain is a subjective sensory and emotional experience that varies considerably across individuals and can be difficult to communicate. We investigated whether complementary autonomic signals could support objective assessment of responses during dental examination. Forty-nine patients underwent cold pulp testing, yielding no-response, mild-response, and intense-response conditions. The framework integrated ECG-derived skin nerve activity (SKNA) and R-R intervals (RRI), together with electrodermal activity (EDA), using temporal convolutional network encoders with attention-based mid-level fusion. Individual baseline signals and subject-level covariates, including anxiety scores and biological sex, were also incorporated. The framework achieved 80.2% balanced accuracy, 75.2% sensitivity, and 85.2% specificity for binary classification of no response versus mild or intense response. For three-class classification, it achieved 60.0% balanced accuracy and a 58.8% macro-averaged F1 score. Ablation and attention-weight analyses indicated that EDA contributed most strongly to model performance, followed by RRI, while SKNA improved balanced accuracy by approximately five percentage points. Age was significantly associated with model performance. These findings support the feasibility of multimodal autonomic sensing for objective, non-invasive assessment of responses to dental pulp stimulation.
authors: Youngsun Kong; Yubin Choi; Dongjin Song; Dong-Guk Shin; I-Ping Chen; Ki Chon

title: Role of Agentic Artificial Intelligence in Anatomical and Clinical Laboratory
abstract: Background: Laboratory medicine is transitioning from passive machine learning models and static decision-support algorithms toward agentic artificial intelligence (AI)—systems capable of goal-directed autonomy, environmental perception, multi-step reasoning, dynamic tool utilization, and iterative self-correction. This review synthesizes the operational frameworks and clinical implications of agentic AI across anatomical pathology and clinical laboratories (Biochemistry, hematology, microbiology, and molecular diagnostics). In anatomical pathology, multi-agent frameworks optimize whole-slide imaging workflows through adaptive region-of-interest navigation, autonomous pre-screening, automated biomarker quantification, and integrated multi-modal report generation. In clinical laboratories, agentic architectures streamline pre-analytic specimen quality verification, orchestrate real-time delta-check evaluations, resolve atypical hematologic cell flagging, guide microbiology culture plate selection, and automate complex next-generation sequencing variant curation. By interconnecting Laboratory Information Systems, digital instrumentation, and electronic health records, multi-agent networks bridge data silos to enable cross-disciplinary diagnostic synthesis. Despite substantial gains in diagnostic throughput, turnaround times, and quality assurance, clinical implementation is constrained by computational overhead, potential error propagation in reasoning chains, data privacy, and the risk of automated "hallucinations". Addressing these challenges necessitates robust human-in-the-loop oversight, standardized audit trails for decision chains, and evolving regulatory compliance frameworks (FDA, CE-IVDR). Agentic AI represents a paradigm shift from narrow analytical tools to collaborative diagnostic teammates, positioned to elevate precision medicine and operational efficiency while redefining the roles of pathologists and laboratory scientists.
authors: Vibhav Nigam; Atulya; Nidhi Mathur; Dilutpal Sharma

title: Advances in Integrated Diagnostics: Innovation and Translation of Laboratory Diagnostic Technologies
abstract: Integrated diagnostics is reshaping modern laboratory medicine by shifting diagnostic practice from fragmented test utilization toward a clinically oriented, data-driven, and patient-centered model. In this review, we summarize the conceptual foundations, technological advances, and translational challenges of integrated laboratory diagnostics. We propose a five-dimensional framework—intelligence, timeliness, accuracy, standardization, and interdisciplinary integration—to describe the core attributes of this emerging paradigm. Within this framework, diagnostic innovation is driven by the convergence of multiple enabling technologies, including liquid biopsy, mass spectrometry, high-throughput and single-cell sequencing, spatial multi-omics, digital pathology, point-of-care testing, organoid models, microfluidics, and interoperable digital infrastructure. Together, these advances support a transition from isolated result generation to dynamic, contextualized, and actionable diagnostic insights, thereby promoting earlier detection, more precise risk stratification, individualized therapeutic guidance, and longitudinal health monitoring. We further discuss the major barriers to clinical translation, including technical and data complexity, limited evidence for clinical utility, workflow integration challenges, and the need for systemic transformation in workforce training, governance, and equitable implementation. Overall, integrated laboratory diagnostics represents a transformative direction for laboratory medicine and precision healthcare. Its successful adoption will depend on coordinated progress in evidence generation, interoperability, and multidisciplinary collaboration, ultimately enabling a more predictive, preventive, personalized, and participatory diagnostic future.
authors: Sergio Bernardini; Jun Zhang

title: AI Rickshaw: A Secure, Geofenced, Solar-Assisted Autonomous Electric Rickshaw for Bangladesh and the Displacement Risk to the Lowest-Income Transport Workers
abstract: Bangladesh moves on rickshaws: a quarter of Dhaka's trips are made by cycle or battery-assisted rickshaw, and one to two million battery-run three-wheelers in the capital each support a driver from one of Bangladesh's lowest-income informal transport workforces. This article presents AI Rickshaw, a reference design for a driverless, app-summoned, solar-assisted electric rickshaw (AIR-1) that keeps the traditional three-wheel form, and uses it as a Bangladesh-specific case study in embodied artificial intelligence. Four contributions are made. First, a reference architecture adapted to lane-less, low-speed, high-density traffic. Second, software-enforced traffic compliance: geofenced operation in which highways, restricted roads, wrong-way movement and out-of-zone trips cannot be planned or executed, so that regulation becomes executable rather than merely instructive. Third, an integrated cyber-physical security architecture for theft, tampering, unauthorised control and passenger emergencies, in which a hard-wired safety microcontroller is the sole validated actuator gateway, so that compromise of the back end does not directly confer actuator authority. Fourth, an argument, with scenario evidence, that embodied AI, the combination of perception, robotics, electric actuation and digital platforms, can threaten the lowest-income manual occupations and not only knowledge work: under the base adoption scenario, substantial displacement of Dhaka's drivers could occur by 2041, and a just-transition framework of a per-vehicle-day levy, garage franchising, microfinance co-ownership and evidence-gated deployment is proposed. Solar energy is treated as assisting, not primary, supply. No physical prototype has yet been built; every quantitative value carries its evidence type, and the next phase is a hardware prototype validated in a private geofenced environment.
authors: Md Israfeel

title: An Autonomous, Continuously-Learning Framework for Real-Time Cyber-Physical Threat Prevention in Legacy SCADA Systems
abstract: Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA) systems remain the operational backbone of critical infrastructure, yet a vast installed base of legacy deployments was engineered for availability and determinism rather than security. These systems typically lack transport encryption, device authentication, and message integrity, and their long service lives and safetycertified configurations make them difficult or impossible to retrofit with conventional cryptographic controls. Signature-based and statically configured intrusion detection cannot keep pace with the concept drift, process reconfiguration, and novel attack techniques that characterize modern industrial threats. This paper proposes an autonomous, continuously-learning anomalydetection framework that treats real-time threat prevention as an adaptive, resilience-oriented process rather than a fixed rule set. The framework is built on a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) Autoencoder that learns the temporal signature of normal process behavior and flags deviations through reconstruction error, and it is organized into three cooperating components: a dataacquisition and preprocessing pipeline that harmonizes heterogeneous logs and protocol exchanges; a detection engine that scores multivariate time series without exhaustive labels; and an alerting, interpretation, and semi-automated response layer that supports operators. A closed feedback loop incrementally updates the notion of “normal” to track sensor drift and control-loop tuning while remaining sensitive to low-and-slow intrusions. We validate the design on a simulated legacy water-treatment SCADA case derived from the SWaT testbed and augmented with synthetic Modbus/TCP anomalies, achieving an F1 score above 0.92 with sub-second detection latency. The contribution is a proactive, deployable defense for critical infrastructure that strengthens cyberphysical resilience without costly hardware replacement.
authors: Chukwunenye Amadi
venue: WORLD JOURNAL OF INNOVATION AND MODERN TECHNOLOGY

title: Robotics and digital automation in general dentistry: A comprehensive review
abstract: Robotics and digital automation are rapidly transforming modern dentistry by enhancing precision, efficiency, and patient outcomes across multiple specialties. These technologies are increasingly applied in implantology, endodontics, prosthodontics, orthodontics, periodontology, and oral and maxillofacial surgery, improving procedural accuracy, reducing operator fatigue, and ensuring consistent clinical results. Robotic-assisted implant placement achieves submillimeter accuracy, while AI-driven endodontic systems enhance canal preparation and irrigation. Automation in prosthodontics and orthodontics streamlines appliance fabrication, and emerging robotic tools support minimally invasive periodontal and maxillofacial procedures. Continued research, clinical validation, and cost-effective implementation strategies are essential to fully realize the potential of robotics in general dental practice.
authors: Rana Rakha; Dr. Shilpi Deshpande; Yuktha Ameersheti; Ebtsam Ben Zeglam; Salma Ashna Jurat; Salma Ashna Jurat; Latifa Elbanna; Sandeep Singh
venue: Southeast Asian Journal of Case Report and Review

title: Ideas and Perspectives: Value and efficiency of ocean sample return and laboratory analysis: Key analytes are orders of magnitude rarer than a needle in a haystack
abstract: Abstract. There is a pressing need to understand how the oceans are responding to human perturbations, yet their vastness poses a considerable challenge. The development and deployment of biologically and ecologically relevant in situ sensors are frequently invoked as a means to improve this understanding; however, there are still relatively few sensors for these parameters due to the analytical challenges involved in their measurement. Specifically, many analytes of interest are orders of magnitude rarer by mass than a needle in a haystack (e.g., dissolved iron and eDNA are 104 to 108 times rarer), and this scarcity creates challenges involving preconcentration, interfering elements or compounds, and analytical methods difficult to perform underwater. While sensor development is important, the role of sample collection and return is also an important, yet oft overlooked, complement for studying ocean change and is ripe for additional development. Laboratory analyses of returned samples can be high throughput for challenging analytes like micronutrients and omics parameters, and these techniques are operational now. Moreover, sample return allows parallel analyses and archiving through splitting of sample material. Similar to human health diagnostics, laboratory analyses can provide ocean health diagnostic capabilities showing how ecosystems are responding, complementing sensor-based vital sign measurements indicating environmental change. Together, these properties make sample collection and return a critical component for achieving the global ocean coverage needed to capture the environmental changes well underway today, and this approach should continue to be factored into ocean observing strategies.
authors: Mak A. Saito; Matthew R. McIlvin; Annette F. Govindarajan; J. A. Breier

title: Entity-aware pathology workflow informatics: Structured evidence mapping and a reference architecture for governed orchestration
abstract: Objective To map evidence relevant to representing and governing pathology workflows spanning cases, specimens, blocks, slides, scans, and reports, and to derive a reference architecture. Methods We performed structured evidence mapping with purposive horizon scanning. Searches of Scopus, PubMed, and IEEE Xplore yielded 74 primary database records; Google Scholar and citation tracking contributed 24 supplementary records. Each record contributed one tuple across data acquisition, control-flow reconfiguration, execution autonomy, and validation environment (D1–D4), an author-developed operational taxonomy. Unretained historical search details are reported as a reproducibility constraint, not reconstructed as original methods. Results The 98-record evidence base spans 1993–2026. Within the 74-record primary corpus, 47 records had dashboard-level execution; validation was split between real-world deployment (26) and conceptual evidence (25). Under study-defined filters, 8/74 records met all 4 minimum capability conditions, 2/74 also showed closed-loop physical actuation, and 1/74 combined full autonomy with real-world deployment. These study-defined filters derive from the original single-reviewer D1–D4 coding. An independent blinded 50-record verification yielded 81.6% inclusion agreement (κ = 0.627) and 80.0% exact D1–D4 field agreement, but did not constitute full-corpus independent reproduction. Supplementary records informed emerging automation requirements. The mapped gaps informed an architecture comprising semantic perception, entity-aware process state, bounded orchestration, pre-action command governance, governed actuation, and conditional local execution support; a safety-and-constraints sandbox is one candidate realization of the governance function. Conclusion The architecture is an evidence-derived design target, not a deployed or validated system. Evaluation should test event provenance, case-to-slide relationships, robustness to missing or shifted inputs, command constraints, human override, and staged operational performance before autonomy claims.
authors: Ao Li; Peter Oloughlin; Lin Yue; Wei Emma Zhang; Bernadette Swart; Weitong Chen

title: Engineering Construction and Risk Management Practice of Intelligent Rail Logistics System in Multi Building Tertiary A Hospital
abstract: To meet the requirements for the high‑quality development of public hospitals and solve practical problems such as low efficiency of in‑hospital material transportation, high labor costs and heavy pressure of nosocomial infection control in multi‑building tertiary‑A hospitals, Chengdu Hospital of Integrated Traditional Chinese and Western Medicine has launched the reconstruction‑and‑expansion project of an intelligent rail‑logistics system. As an intelligent renovation project constructed under the premise of uninterrupted medical services, it is restricted by multiple factors including existing building conditions, nosocomial‑infection control requirements and extreme weather, with engineering risks running through the whole project lifecycle. Combined with project practice, this paper carries out whole‑lifecycle risk identification and assessment, establishes a risk matrix, formulates corresponding countermeasures, and builds a closed‑loop management system of “risk identification‑assessment‑disposal‑review”. Risk control is implemented through multi‑party collaboration, phased construction, on‑site operation and maintenance, special training and emergency disposal. A total of 48 stations are planned with a total rail length of 2567 m, among which 32 stations have been put into operation. The system completes an average of 320 delivery tasks per day, with a 30‑minute task completion rate of 93 %. The labor cost for full‑time delivery staff is reduced by 50 %. The construction objectives of cost reduction and efficiency improvement, nosocomial‑infection prevention and refined operation of intelligent logistics support have been achieved. Practice proves that whole‑lifecycle engineering risk management is critical to the successful implementation of hospital intelligent reconstruction‑and‑expansion projects, and can provide practical references for similar domestic hospital intelligent‑logistics projects.
authors: Hong Lyu

title: Integration of liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry into total laboratory automation: technical challenges and clinical advantages
abstract: The clinical laboratory is undergoing a paradigm shift toward the integration of liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry(MS) into Total Laboratory Automation workflows. While historically relegated to specialized satellite units due to manual pre-analytical requirements, recent technological advancements have enabled the development of fully automated, 'sample-to-result' MS modules. This review provides an authoritative analysis of the technical integration of systems such as the Roche cobas® i 601 and Shimadzu CLAM-2040 in core laboratories. We examine the role of intelligent middleware and artificial intelligence-assisted algorithms in ensuring standardized data validation and quality control tracking and real-time operational monitoring. Furthermore, we evaluate the clinical impact of this integration on diagnostic accuracy for low-concentration analytes in endocrinology and therapeutic drug monitoring. By transitioning from batch-based processing to continuous automated streams, MS establishes itself as a robust, high-throughput tool for routine clinical diagnostics.
authors: Carlos José Sánchez Ovejero; Sergio Luis Lima; Irene Chaves Coira; Alfonso Rey Catena

title: Self‐Feeding Living Materials Enabled by Cell Responsive Glycogen Nanoparticles as Metabolic Batteries
abstract: Scaling engineered living materials to clinically relevant dimensions is limited by diffusion-dependent depletion of oxygen and nutrients, which rapidly induces metabolic failure. We introduce glycogen as a nutritional nanoparticle that provides cell-mediated, autonomous nutrient release to support long-term survival under extreme metabolic stress. We demonstrate that human mesenchymal stromal cells (hMSCs) survive for weeks in anoxia and serum deprivation when provided extracellular glycogen. Contrary to long-held assumptions, hMSCs secrete glycogen-degrading enzymes, enabling cell-density-controlled extracellular glycogenolysis and sustained release of glucose and metabolic intermediates, positioning glycogen as the first-of-its-kind metabolic battery. This cell-responsive process maintains metabolic activity, limits glycolytic acidosis, and enhances pro-angiogenic signaling. To translate this mechanism into a versatile materials platform, we engineered core-shell dextran-tyramine microcapsules that stably encapsulate glycogen while permitting diffusion of enzymes and degradation products. Integrated into centimeter-scale GelMA constructs, these microcapsules maintained hMSC viability and function for at least 1 month under anoxia. In vivo, glycogen-loaded implants promote deep cellular infiltration, enhanced matrix remodeling, increased M2 macrophage polarization, and orchestrated accelerated vascularization. This work establishes the novel concept of glycogen-based nutritional nanoparticles as metabolic batteries to endow engineered tissues with autonomous self-feeding capacity, enabling scalable and functional living materials for regenerative medicine and related technologies.
authors: Melvin Gurian; Niels G. A. Willemen; Isa Robin Porsul; Nicole Joy Bassous; Jarno Hiemstra; Yu Na; Debby Gawlitta; Su Ryon Shin; Jeroen Leijten

title: A Calibrated Lightweight CNN Ensemble with CIELABCLAHE Preprocessing for White Blood Cell Classification and Hematological Disorder Screening
abstract: White blood cell (WBC) classification is a clinically critical task in hematology, underpinning the diagnosis of blood malignancies, including leukemia, as well as infections and immune disorders. Accurate automated WBC differential counting is essential for early detection of conditions such as chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) and acute myeloid leukemia (AML), where abnormal leukocyte counts and morphology are primary diagnostic indicators. Manual differential counting is time-consuming, subjective, and prone to inter-observer variability. This paper proposes a weighted ensemble framework combining three lightweight pretrained convolutional neural networks (CNNs): EfficientNet-B0, MobileNetV3-Small, and MobileNetV3-Large for automated four-class WBC classification on Paul Mooney’s Blood Cell Images dataset (BCCD, Kaggle). A standardized preprocessing pipeline was employed to enhance nuclear contrast and normalize photometric variability. Each backbone was finetuned under a two-phase transfer-learning protocol with AdamW optimization and cosine annealing scheduling. Model evaluation was conducted via stratified 3-fold cross-validation, and ensemble predictions were aggregated using accuracy-weighted soft voting. The proposed ensemble achieved a classification accuracy of 98.57%, a weighted F1-score of 0.9857, a Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC) of 0.9810, and a mean AUC of 0.9994. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of ensemble-based transfer learning combined with targeted preprocessing for robust, well-calibrated WBC classification, with direct applicability to clinical laboratory automation.
authors: Aya Achir; Ilham Battas; Ikram Debbarh; Hicham Medromi; Fouad Moutaouakkil
venue: International Journal of Online and Biomedical Engineering (iJOE)

title: Development and validation of multiple machine learning models for identifying factors associated with walking ability in ischemic stroke patients: a single-center retrospective study with SHAP approach
abstract: Objectives: The aim of this study was to develop and validate machine learning (ML) models that integrate inflammatory biomarkers with clinical indicators to identify factors associated with walking ability in patients with ischemic stroke (IS). The major research question was which ML model achieves optimal discriminative performance for gait impairment in IS patients, and which factors are the key factors of walking ability in this population. Methods: This retrospective cohort study enrolled 1,650 patients diagnosed with ischemic stroke. The participants were randomly allocated to a training set (70%) and a validation set (30%). Data on clinical, laboratory, and imaging variables were collected. Feature selection was performed using the Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator (LASSO) regression, the Boruta algorithm, and logistic regression. Six machine learning models were developed. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis was applied to the best-performing model. Results: Five significant factors were screened: the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR), age, gender, occipital lobe and frontal lobe lesions. Random forest (RF) achieved optimal performance with an AUC of 0.868 in the training set and 0.681 in the test set. SHAP analysis prioritized NLR as the top contributor. Conclusions: The ML models show preliminary promise as screening tools for early risk stratification for gait impairment in IS patients.
authors: Jianying Qiu; Xiaoguang Yang; Meng Guo; Wei Guo; XinYi Guo; Xiping Jia; Qihan Sun

title: Human-In-The-Loop Decision Systems: Advances and Future Directions
abstract: Human-in-the-loop (HITL) decision systems combine algorithmic inference with human judgment so that people supervise, correct, and complement automated components rather than being replaced by them. As machine learning is embedded in consequential decisions across finance, public administration, and security operations, the question is no longer whether to automate but how to allocate authority between people and machines so that the joint system outperforms either alone. This paper synthesizes advances in HITL decision systems and sets out a research agenda. We first clarify the HITL concept and situate it on the automation spectrum, drawing on classical models of levels of automation and function allocation. We then review four intersecting streams of progress: interaction paradigms and active learning that let people shape models efficiently; explanation and calibrated trust, where explainable AI and trust-calibration research aim to align reliance with actual system reliability; task allocation and adaptive autonomy grounded in mixed initiative interaction; and domain applications in financial analytics, digital public services, and operational risk and cybersecurity. A described taxonomy organizes recurring HITL patterns by the locus and timing of human involvement. We next examine open challenges, automation bias and algorithm aversion, cognitive load and vigilance decrement, diffuse accountability, and the immaturity of evaluation methods that measure joint human-AI performance rather than model accuracy alone. Finally, we propose a forward agenda emphasizing calibrated-reliance metrics, adaptive and learnable task allocation, human-centered explanation, sociotechnical accountability, and rigorous mixed-methods evaluation. We argue that treating the human and the model as a single joint cognitive system is the central design principle for the next generation of decision systems.
authors: Ashore-Onisemo Funmilayo
venue: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF SOCIAL SCIENCES AND MANAGEMENT RESEARCH

title: Head-to-head comparison of MRI-based PI-RR scoring system and 68 Ga-PSMA-PET/CT: enhancing prostate cancer recurrence detection after radical prostatectomy
abstract: PURPOSE: To compare the diagnostic performance of MRI using the PI-RR scoring system and PSMA-PET/CT in detecting prostate cancer (PCa) local recurrence after radical prostatectomy (RP), and to identify clinical and imaging variables independently associated with recurrence. MATERIALS AND METHODS: This retrospective, multicenter study evaluated 119 patients with suspected PCa recurrence who underwent both MRI and PSMA-PET/CT; MRI was performed within a time window ranging from up to 3 months before to a maximum of 1 month after the PET/CT examination; the time range was defined within MDTs. Both radiologists and nuclear medicine physicians were blinded to clinical and opposite imaging data during image interpretation. Exclusion criteria included insufficient follow-up, recent pelvic radiation (within 6 months), and history of hormone therapy. Reference standard was defined using histopathologic findings, follow-up imaging, or clinical response to treatment. Sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, and accuracy were calculated. The Cohen's kappa coefficient was used to determine inter-reader agreement. Univariable and multivariable logistic regression analyses were performed. RESULTS: MRI, considering a PI-RR ≥ 3, detected recurrence in 69 patients versus 48 with PSMA-PET/CT (p = 0.006). MRI showed significantly higher sensitivity (86%, 95% CI 75-92% vs. 71%, 95% CI 59-80%; p = 0.03) and a trend toward higher specificity (78%, 95% CI 65-87% vs. 52%, 95% CI 39-65%; p = 0.06), PPV (74% vs. 51%), NPV (89% vs. 73%). Overall accuracy was also superior for MRI (81%, 95% CI 74-87% vs. 63%, 95% CI 54-71%). ROC analysis confirmed a higher AUC for MRI (0.87, 95% CI 0.80-0.93) compared with PSMA-PET/CT (0.62, 95% CI 0.52-0.72; ΔAUC = 0.25, p < 0.001). Multivariable analysis showed that only age (p = 0.002) and PI-RR score ≥ 3 (p = 0.001) were independently correlated with recurrence. Postoperative risk grouping was correlated only at univariable analysis. Among the 119 included patients, histopathologic confirmation was available in 3% (n = 4), treatment response (either biochemical or imaging based) in 31% (n = 37), follow-up with imaging in 33% (n = 39), and clinical-laboratory follow-up in 33% (n = 39).The median follow-up was 12 months (IQR, 9-18). The effective recurrence rate was 58%. CONCLUSIONS: MRI demonstrated strong diagnostic performance in detecting prostate cancer local recurrence. These findings suggest that MRI may be particularly useful for rule out local recurrence in low-risk patients, while PET/CT could be more appropriate for rule in, both local and distant in higher-risk patients. However, this proposed risk-adapted imaging strategy should be considered hypothesis-generating and warrants further validation through prespecified risk-stratified analyses. Limitations include the retrospective design, the composite reference standard, and the relatively high recurrence prevalence, which may have influenced predictive values.
authors: Ludovica Laschena; Martina Pecoraro; Emanuele Messina; Marco Bicchetti; Antonella Borrelli; Ailin Dehghanpour; Francesca Mezzapesa; Nicholas Landini; Giuseppe De Vincentis; Valeria Panebianco

title: WaveFusionNet: frequency-gated spatial modulation and Wavelet Energy-Guided Contrastive Learning for dual-branch malaria cell classification
abstract: Automated malaria diagnosis using microscopic blood smear images has emerged as an effective alternative to manual examination; however, existing deep learning approaches predominantly rely on spatial-domain representations and conventional optimization objectives, limiting their ability to exploit complementary spectral information and discriminate challenging samples. This paper proposes WaveFusionNet, a novel dual-branch deep learning framework that jointly learns spatial and frequency-domain representations for robust malaria cell classification. The proposed architecture introduces two original contributions. First, a Frequency-Gated Spatial Modulation (FGSM) module computes wavelet detail-energy maps to generate adaptive spatial gates, enabling frequency information to selectively enhance informative spatial features while suppressing irrelevant background responses. Second, a Wavelet Energy-Guided Contrastive Loss (WEGCL) exploits eight-dimensional wavelet energy signatures to identify spectrally hard positive and negative pairs, thereby strengthening feature discrimination through adaptive contrastive learning. Furthermore, a Cross-Domain Attention Fusion module effectively integrates complementary spatial and frequency representations using multi-head cross-attention, while Adaptive Channel-Spatial Attention dynamically balances channel-wise and spatial feature refinement throughout the network. Extensive experiments on the benchmark NIH Malaria Cell Images dataset (27,558 images) demonstrate that WaveFusionNet achieves 98.47% accuracy, 98.60% recall, and an AUC of 0.9978, consistently outperforming eight state-of-the-art deep learning models. Five-fold cross-validation confirms excellent statistical robustness, and Grad-CAM visualizations verify that the proposed framework accurately localizes clinically relevant parasitic regions. Despite its superior predictive capability, the model remains computationally efficient, with only 15.1 million parameters and an inference latency of 7.2 ms, making it well-suited for real-time deployment in resource-constrained point-of-care environments. The proposed WaveFusionNet provides an effective and interpretable spatial-frequency learning paradigm that advances automated malaria diagnosis through synergistic feature fusion and wavelet-guided representation learning.
authors: Naif Alzahrani; Sandeep Kumar Thota; Ala Alarood; Kemal Polat

title: AI-Assisted Risk and Incident Analysis: Advances and Future Opportunities
abstract: Operational risk and security incidents now unfold across distributed, cloud-native estates that generate volumes of telemetry no human team can manually triage at speed. Over the past decade, artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) have moved from experimental log-mining prototypes to production components of security operations centres, site reliability engineering practices, and enterprise risk functions. This paper synthesises the advances that have made AIassisted risk and incident analysis viable and examines the opportunities and limitations that will shape the next phase of adoption. We organise the state of the art into five capability areas: anomaly and detection analytics over logs, metrics, and traces; alert triage, deduplication, and correlation; natural language processing (NLP) and large language models (LLMs) for incident summarisation, knowledge retrieval, and postmortem authoring; automation and orchestration of response workflows; and human–AI collaboration in the analyst loop. We map these capabilities to established incident-handling and risk-management frameworks and present a structured capabilities table describing typical inputs, methods, and outputs. We then interrogate the open challenges that temper enthusiasm: model hallucination and reliability, the sensitivity and governance of incident data, the immaturity of evaluation methodology, and the operational hazards of over-automation. Finally, we propose a research agenda spanning benchmarking, retrieval-grounded and explainable reasoning, evaluation of human–AI teams, and resilienceaware automation. We argue that the near-term value of AI in this domain lies less in autonomous decision-making than in augmenting scarce expert attention, and that trustworthy deployment depends on grounding, evaluation, and human oversight rather than on model scale alone.
authors: Uchechi Mary-Linda Unamma
venue: WORLD JOURNAL OF INNOVATION AND MODERN TECHNOLOGY

title: A Scalable Multi-Sensor Vision Framework for Automated Bat Monitoring and 3D Habitat Analysis
abstract: Automated wildlife monitoring systems are essential for studying bat populations in natural environments, where nocturnal behavior, high flight speeds, and limited illumination make conventional observation difficult. This paper presents a modular multi-sensor vision system that integrates RGB, near-infrared (NIR), and depth cameras for automated bat monitoring. The proposed architecture consists of one main module and two secondary modules that can be configured into multiple operating modes according to monitoring requirements. The main module operates independently to perform real-time habitat reconstruction using an integrated depth camera or bat detection using a YOLO-based model. When combined with one secondary module, it forms a stereo vision system for three-dimensional localization; when combined with both secondary modules, it generates panoramic images that substantially expand the field of view for monitoring large cave entrances and other complex environments. The proposed modular architecture enables flexible deployment while supporting multiple sensing configurations within a single platform. The modular design provides scalability, geometric consistency through multi-sensor calibration, and flexible deployment, enabling accurate bat detection, habitat reconstruction, and wide-area monitoring within a unified sensing framework. The proposed system provides a versatile and scalable solution for adapting wildlife monitoring to different environmental conditions and observation scenarios. Experimental results demonstrate a detection precision of 0.893, a panoramic field of view of 119°, and real-time processing at 60 fps, validating the effectiveness of the proposed modular architecture.
authors: José-Ángel Arroyo-Romero; Isabel Bárcenas-Reyes; Juan B. Hurtado‐Ramos; Francisco-Javier Ornelas-Rodríguez; Erick-Alejandro González-Barbosa; Alfonso Ramírez-Pedraza; José‐Joel González‐Barbosa

title: Augmented and mixed reality as auxiliary tools in dental procedures and their integration with artificial intelligence: A scoping review
abstract: OBJECTIVES: To map and synthesize the scientific evidence regarding the use of Augmented Reality (AR) and Mixed Reality (MR) as auxiliary tools in dental procedures, and to examine the extent to which Artificial Intelligence (AI) has been integrated into these workflows. DATA: A scoping review was conducted in accordance with the PRISMA-ScR guidelines and the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) recommendations. The study selection and data extraction processes were carried out by two independent reviewers, with disagreements resolved by consensus. SOURCES: Searches were performed in PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science for studies published up to June 2025. STUDY SELECTION: Fifteen studies were included from a total of 1,457 records identified. Most of the evidence was concentrated in implant dentistry, where MR-based dynamic navigation achieved sub-millimetric accuracy (e.g., three-dimensional entry deviation of 0.417 mm) and outperformed the freehand technique. Improvements in angular accuracy (up to 72% among inexperienced operators) were observed in orthodontic mini-implant placement, and more conservative tissue removal was reported in endodontic access and in tooth preparation. In zygomatic implant placement, however, the freehand technique was not surpassed in apical or angular accuracy, and accuracy improved only when robotic stabilization was added. Artificial Intelligence was identified in a minority of the included studies and, where present, was restricted to preparatory stages of the workflow, namely automated segmentation, image registration, and planning support, rather than to intraoperative execution. CONCLUSIONS: AR and MR were applied predominantly as intraoperative visualization and navigation aids and showed accuracy superior to freehand execution, whereas AI functioned as an enabling technology confined to the preparatory stages of the workflow. Given the predominance of in vitro and proof-of-concept designs, these findings indicate technical feasibility rather than established clinical effectiveness, and multicenter randomized trials with independent validation of the systems remain necessary before clinical adoption can be established.
authors: MATHEUS PINÓS; Newton Sesma; Giovani Flach; Eduardo Mukai

title: Precision Nutrition and Nutrigenomic Intelligence for Microbiome-Aware Diet Design, Metabolic Health and Healthy Longevity
abstract: Abstract Precision nutrition increasingly requires an integrated analytical architecture capable of connecting dietary exposure, genomic and multi-omic variation, microbiome ecology, metabolic phenotype, longitudinal biosensing and the social conditions that shape adherence. This book develops such an architecture from the supplied research corpus, treating personalized diet design as a sequence of representation, inference, prediction, causal evaluation, adaptive monitoring and governance decisions. Because the source set contains relatively few studies that are explicitly microbiome-specific, microbiome-aware reasoning is developed by synthesizing the corpus on omics, clinical artificial intelligence, high-dimensional learning, causal inference, wearable biosensing, digital twins, functional data analysis and trustworthy deployment. The manuscript advances five linked layers: research design under uncertainty; statistical explanation and heterogeneous treatment-effect estimation; machine learning for multimodal prediction and generalization; scalable data engineering, edge analytics and metabolic digital twins; and translation into metabolic health, healthy longevity, resilient food systems and policy. Across these layers, the emphasis is on traceable assumptions, calibration, transportability, subgroup evaluation, reproducibility and human oversight. The resulting framework is intended for researchers, clinicians, nutrition professionals, digital-health developers, food-system actors and policymakers seeking a rigorous basis for microbiome-aware diet intelligence across diverse global contexts. Keywords precision nutrition, nutrigenomics, microbiome, multi-omics, diet design, metabolic health, healthy longevity, digital twins, wearable biosensing, causal inference, heterogeneous treatment effects, functional data analysis, graph neural networks, topological data analysis, foundation models, generative omics, multimodal learning, MLOps, edge intelligence, trustworthy AI, health equity, food-system resilience, reproducibility, personalized prevention
authors: Murali Krishna Pasupuleti

title: Editorial: Socio-legal, ethical, technical and medical considerations on neuroprivacy and brain-machine interaction technologies in the era of A.I.
abstract: The rapid convergence of neurotechnology and artificial intelligence (AI) has moved beyond the isolation of clinical laboratories and IT factories to become a transformative force capable, in the long-term, of redefining the human experience. In the wake of brain-machine interaction technologies, human and cognitive enhancement and even transhumanism perspectives, this evolution has given rise to the concept of the hybrid mind, a state where biological cognitive systems merge seamlessly with artificial ones, blurring traditional boundaries of identity, agency, autonomy, and consciousness. While these advances offer unprecedented potential to restore sensory and motor functions, they simultaneously challenge our foundational understandings of cognitive liberty, mental integrity, neuroethics and conventional privacy paradigms. This Research Topic, hosted by Frontiers in Human Dynamics -Digital Impacts and cross-listed across seven participating journals, includingFrontiers in Sociology, Neurology, and Neurorobotics, serves as a multidisciplinary research collection that aims to connect different fields and backgrounds with a common frame. It also archives the overall findings that emerged from the international conference "The Hybrid Mind: Ethics and Regulation of Intelligent Neuroprostheses", that took place in October 2023 in Berlin, Germany. Under the stewardship of the editors spanning legal, ethical, medical, and IT backgrounds, the collection features the work of 39 authors, and reflects a rigorous selection process, resulting in a competitive acceptance rate of 46%. In terms of typology of scientific research, the contributions, from 3 reviews, 2 conceptual analyses and 1 study protocol to 3 perspectives and 2 original research papers, paint an articulated, yet still homogeneous spectrum of different research perspectives that pivot around the neuroprivacy topic. The impact of this collection is already evident from the numbers of citations, research topic views, article views, and article downloads.The 11 articles in this collection can be organised into four thematic clusters (plus one focus) that reveal a productive tension between the drive for therapeutic "super-human" capabilities and the necessity of safeguarding the "most intimate personal corner": the mind.The collection provides a firm grounding in current medical progress, establishing a baseline for the technical capabilities that now interact with the human mind. Deng and colleagues provide a comprehensive twenty-year bibliometric analysis of Vagus Nerve Stimulation (VNS) for stroke rehabilitation, documenting a clear transition from basic pathophysiological research toward translational studies focused on neuroplasticity. Their findings highlight how non-invasive methods, such as transauricular VNS, are gaining traction as safer and more cost-effective alternatives to surgical intervention. Complementing this technical trajectory, Kim et al. present a double-blinded randomised control pilot trial protocol utilising the RecoveriX PRO system. Their work aims to verify that motor imagery-contingent neurofeedback is superior to sham feedback in subacute stroke rehabilitation, asserting that the closed-loop connection between intention and feedback is essential for the effective reorganisation of neural circuits. The trial aims to resolve a current research gap by directly comparing the superiority of "real BCI" (MI-contingent feedback) over "sham BCI" (MIirrelevant feedback) specifically for patients in the subacute phase of stroke. The protocol uniquely combines clinical evaluations with neurophysiological tools like EEG (functional connectivity) and TMS (cortical excitability) to assess brain reorganization from the cerebral cortex down to the endeffector. Liang expands this technical scope into the aesthetic and cognitive realms, surveying how machine learning can decode and generate music based on emotional and cognitive states. The findings suggest that ML interpretations of "cognitive harmony" must account for complex cultural and individual variables, as a user's response to music is an interplay of cultural background and unique image-thinking processes. This research suggests a profound potential for AI to harmonise minds and machines through "picture-thinking" processes, essentially utilising music as a universal language to bridge the gap between human emotion and algorithmic interpretation. While these studies focus essentially on the medical fields, their findings also enable interlinked ethical and legal considerations to emerge precisely around new implications for neuroprivacy -especially concerning neuro-data protection-and cognitive liberties.A significant portion of the collection grapples with the high-profile entry of private entities into the neurotechnology sector, most notably represented by Neuralink. Lavazza and a multidisciplinary team of co-authors provide a critical conceptual analysis of Neuralink's brain-computer interfaces (BCIs), acknowledging technical milestones such as device miniaturisation and robotic implantation techniques. However, they raise a sharp "neuroskeptical alarm" concerning ethics aspects of neurotechnologies, as found in the Media, regarding the company's deviation from established scientific norms, specifically criticising the initial failure to register clinical trials in public databases like ClinicalTrials.gov., although the company never had the intention to be a public or academic project. Thus, it is not surprising that they do not adhere to these conventions. However, this lack of transparency undermines the ability of the scientific community to evaluate safety and efficacy, highlighting a dangerous precedent where technological enthusiasm may bypass the ethical accountability required for such intimate human-machine integrations. Indeed, the key finding is that Neuralink's practice of announcing progress via social media rather than peer-reviewed journals, and its initial failure to register its clinical trial, deviates from established scientific and ethical norms, undermining public trust and accountability. The article further highlights that Neuralink is unique because it explicitly aims to go beyond therapeutic restoration to "unlock human potential" in healthy individuals, which raises urgent questions about labour competition (an aspect precisely addressed by Muhl and Andorno), positional advantage, and the creation of "posthuman" entities.As neurodevices migrate from clinical settings to the consumer market, the collection identifies severe regulatory gaps and emerging threats to individual liberty. As mentioned, Muhl and Andorno explore the prospect of neurosurveillance in the workplace, arguing that employers using EEG-based devices to monitor fatigue could inadvertently gain access to subconscious processing over which individuals have no mindful control. They maintain that the inherent power imbalance in employment relationships makes "informed consent" a myth, as workers may feel coerced into monitoring to avoid professional detriment. Muhl explores further these positions, arguing that brain data should be legally classified as a special category of sensitive data. Because this data is often generated with no individual awareness both of the data generated or their processing by third parties, and contains information about health status (such as neurological disorders), it warrants the highest level of protection under GDPR. Wilkins et al. shift this concern to the regulatory level, identifying a critical lack of cybersecurity expertise within Institutional Review Boards (IRBs). Current regulatory mechanisms focus heavily on pre-market safety but are inadequate for implantable BCIs, which may induce neural and personality changes that unfold over extended periods and require lifelong followup. The paper identifies severe cybersecurity risks unique to BCIs, such as "neuronal flooding" or "jamming", where a hacker could maliciously perform "neuronal cyberattacks" to alter a user's behaviour, neural activity, and steal intimate personal information. They thus warn that the riskbenefit ratio of BCI research is becoming increasingly difficult to quantify. Kamenjasevic adds to this complexity by examining mood enhancement technology (mood HETs), noting that while legal systems are flexible, they lack a precise definition of "data concerning mood", which may leave users vulnerable to workplace monitoring or political exploitation. He argues that such data must be recognised as a special category of personal data to prevent chilling effects on the freedom of thought and to ensure that enhancements are not used to label specific emotional states as unwanted or non-normal. The article clarifies that mood enhancement involves using technology to change affective states "above levels of normality" distinguishing mood as a long-lasting, private, and internal state compared to the more spontaneous and external nature of emotion. The author also advocates that HETs be prescribed by healthcare professionals who can monitor side effects and provide valid informed consent, rather than being sold as unregulated over-the-counter consumer products.The collection further pushes the boundaries of neuroethics by proposing radical re-evaluations of the law and human ability. Borbón introduces the concept of neuro-abolitionism, suggesting that insights from neuroscience regarding the deterministic or truly random nature of behaviour undermine the traditional assumptions of free will that underpin retributive criminal law. He calls for the abolition of punitive models in favour of restorative justice paradigms that prioritise dignity and acknowledge that behaviour is often socially and culturally situated rather than purely neurobiological. The article contends that the current penal system focuses on holding individuals fully responsible while ignoring the systemic and structural social causes of crime (such as marginalisation and poverty), effectively making the state an accomplice to the conditions that produce deviant behaviour. Thus, the author provocatively proposes a long-term shift toward the total abolition of the prison system, advocating instead for humane alternatives like transdisciplinary understanding (neuroscience, criminology, and sociology), and strictly consensual therapeutic neuro-interventions that respect cognitive liberty. In a similarly visionary perspective, Dezso proposes the concept of "co-ability", arguing that the potency of any physical entity -biological or artificial -is not inherent but is amplified through its distributed network relationships. She advocates for a shift from a "visuocentric" to a "motocentric" focus in perception, where tangible 3D-printed prototypes bridge the communicative gap between abstract information and human physical experience, moving toward the dissolution of human-centred norms, suggesting that sensemaking is most effective when it involves exploratory motor activities like touch and active engagement with the environment. The author argues for digital fabrication and rapid prototyping, which are used to bridge the gap between formless data and material reality, creating tangible media that allow for an action-oriented nonverbal dialog between humans and their data-saturated environments.The Hybrid Mind conference summary, presented by Buthut, Starke, and an international cohort of experts, provides a vital synthesis of the 2023 Berlin conference and serves as one of the collection's ethical anchors. A primary consensus identified is the urgent need for bidirectional BCI technologies to remain strictly focused on medical needs, with a proposed ban on their implantation in healthy populations until long-term well-being and cognitive liberty are guaranteed. The summary introduces the concept of "oblomovization" (a term coined by Niels Birbaumer during the conference), describing a state of lethargy and passivity caused by over-reliance on neurotechnology for daily functions, which must be mitigated through public awareness. Furthermore, the conference participants emphasised that neurotechnology may create instances of existential dependency, particularly when a device becomes integrated into a patient's sense of self. The findings demand a "right to mental self-determination" and a transition toward "soft assembly" mechanisms where distributed competencies are valued over individual ability. Ultimately, the summary calls for a global framework -similar to the one recently issued by UNESCO -that balances rapid innovation with the protection of human rights and dignity, ensuring that neurotechnology remains a benefit to humanity at large rather than a tool for surveillance or control.In general, we would highlight that despite the wealth of data and arguments in this collection, several "unsolved mysteries" remain at the heart of the neuroprivacy debate: what are the long-term post-trial responsibilities of manufacturers when a device becomes an essential part of an individual's identity, but the company ceases operations? Also, as enhancement technologies become increasingly available on the consumer market, who decides (and how) what constitutes "unlocking human potential" versus "distorting behaviour"? And, finally, how can we prevent the of dual-usage of neurotechnology -where media hype and military interests oscillate between fear and enthusiasmfrom dictating global policy?In conclusion, the research presented here indicates that we are entering an era of unprecedented human-machine interaction, with the risk of existential dependency on neurotechnology, which, therefore, necessitates transdisciplinary science discussion (possibly -the editors claim -a new fertile branch for science diplomacy). The collection demonstrates that neuroprivacy cannot be addressed as a series of isolated technical hurdles, because it is a fundamental challenge to human dignity that requires a cohesive legal and ethical framework. We must delve deeper into the multidisciplinary connections between neuroscience, IT, law, and ethics to allow researchers from diverse backgrounds to understand and address these phenomena together. We invite the academic community and policymakers to move away from the intrusive paradigms emerging from for-profit neurodevices development and join the scholars presenting their results in this collection in defining a social framework that protects the sanctity of the mind while responsibly unlocking the hybrid potentials of the future.
authors: Gianluigi M. Riva; Simona Tiribelli; Giovanni Ziccardi; Surjo Raphael Soekadar; Sara Colantonio; Agustí Solanas

title: Building the Rural Nursing Workforce of the Future: Education, Research, and Partnerships to Address Persistent Health Challenges
abstract: Background: Rural populations experience healthcare disparities, including workforce shortages, geographic isolation, limited access to specialty services, and adverse social determinants of health. These challenges are particularly evident in South Dakota, where nearly half of the population resides in rural or frontier communities. Because of these unique challenges associated with rural life, preparing nurses to work in rural America is critical in preparing a workforce capable of meeting the unique healthcare needs of this population. Methods: This article describes how South Dakota State University College of Nursing, located within a rural land-grant institution, has developed and adapted educational programs, workforce initiatives, community partnerships, and re-search programs to address persistent rural health challenges across the state and region. The College of Nursing (CON) includes three campus locations: Brookings, Sioux Falls, and Rapid City and includes undergraduate and graduate nursing education. Nursing education is designed to allow students to blend their nursing education with South Dakota's unique rural environment. Results: The CON offers multiple pathways into the profession, including traditional and accelerated Bachelor of Science in Nursing (BSN) pro-grams, an online BSN option utilizing a train-in-place model, master's-level nursing education and administrator programs, Doctor of Nursing Practice (DNP) programs, and PhD education. Through strategic academic-practice partnerships and federally funded work-force initiatives, the college prepares nurses for rural practice across primary care, acute care, long-term care, and underserved settings. Additional initiatives support Native American student success, rural workforce recruitment and retention, oral health outreach, care coordination for children and youth with special healthcare needs, and research focused on workforce well-being, workplace violence, and healthcare access. Conclusions: A multi-site college of nursing can serve as a model for improving rural healthcare access, strengthening the nursing workforce, and addressing the complex and persistent health needs of rural and frontier populations. South Dakota State Universi-ty CON demonstrates how innovative educational delivery models, community partnerships, and targeted workforce initiatives can contribute to sustainable rural healthcare solutions.
authors: Lea Niederbaumer; Michelle Lichtenberg; Danielle M. Schievelbein; Abby O. Seydel; Nicole Carlson; Theresa Garren-Grubbs; Danielle Currier; Brian Williamson; Amanda Mehlhaff; Marie Schmit; Sarah Mollman

title: Abstracts From the 2026 Health Care Systems Research Network (HCSRN) Annual Conference, Dallas, Texas:How Can Community Mental Health Provision for Working-Age Adults in England Be Improved? An Accelerated Parallelised Realist Literature Review
abstract: Background: Community mental health services in England face persistent challenges in access, capacity, and equity, exacerbated by the COVID-19 pandemic. The 2019 Community Mental Health Framework aimed to deliver integrated, personcentred care, but implementation has been hindered by resource constraints and systemic inequalities. These pressures compromise safety and outcomes, particularly for minoritised groups. Understanding the conditions under which services succeed or fail is critical for improving care delivery and informing strategies that address disparities in mental health systems. Methods: We developed a novel accelerated parallelised realist-informed literature review methodology to deliver this research in under one month to inform policy decision-making by a health regulator in England. We examined contexts and mechanisms influencing safe and effective community mental health provision for working-age adults to identify what worked about existing policies, for whom, and why. Sources included grey literature, systematic searches of Medline and PsycINFO, and expert peer input. Inclusion criteria focused on UK-based studies relevant to adults aged 18-65 accessing community mental health services. Review processes were streamlined to deliver findings within four weeks while maintaining rigour. From 81 sources, we developed initial programme theories and 26 context-mechanism-outcome configurations (CMOCs). Results: Capacity constraints and entrenched inequalities emerged as dominant factors shaping service quality and safety. Strict referral criteria and fragmented care pathways were associated with disengagement and deterioration of patient condition. CMOCs clustered around three themes: learning from practice and safety, medicine optimisation, and research gaps. Key recommendations include to (1) develop culturally appropriate, co-produced measures of risk encompassing patient, public, and systemic perspectives; (2) expand service capacity to reduce transition risks and improve timeliness of care; and (3) strengthen engagement and trust among minoritised communities to address disparities and improve outcomes. Conclusions: Findings highlight the interdependence of patient safety and systemic resilience. Practices that restrict access amplify risks and perpetuate inequities. Implementing these recommendations can help health systems adapt to changing demands, reduce inequalities, and deliver safer, more responsive care for working-age adults. While focused on England, these insights offer transferable lessons for health systems globally seeking to strengthen community mental health provision under resource constraints and evolving challenges.
authors: Justin Avery Aunger; Bianca Ungureanu; Rachel Posaner; Christian Bohm; Ross Millar; S. M. Fenton
