title: Evaluating the rehabilitative and assistive impact of the Agilik exoskeleton: a pre-post single-group study in children with cerebral palsy.
abstract: Cerebral palsy (CP) is a common childhood-onset neurological condition often associated with crouch gait, a pathological walking pattern impairing mobility. Wearable robotic devices are emerging as promising tools for paediatric gait rehabilitation, but evidence on their rehabilitative and assistive effects remains limited. This exploratory study evaluated the rehabilitative and assistive effects of a 10-session training programme using Agilik, a paediatric knee exoskeleton, in children with CP and crouch gait, during level-ground, uphill, and downhill walking. Eight children with CP completed the intervention. Assessments were performed at baseline (T0) and post-intervention (T1), including walking endurance, speed, balance, spasticity, and clinical joint and muscle length assessments. Three-dimensional gait analysis (GRAIL system) quantified sagittal-plane hip, knee, and ankle range of motion during level-ground, uphill, and downhill walking. At T1, joint range of motion was analysed with and without Agilik to assess its assistive effect. User satisfaction was evaluated using the child-adapted QUEST 2.1 questionnaire. Given the exploratory nature of this study, results were interpreted primarily at the individual level using predefined minimal clinically important difference (MCID) thresholds. When clinically relevant changes occurred, improvements were more frequently observed than deteriorations in walking endurance (MCID > 15 m), speed (MCID > 0.1 m/s), muscle lengths (>5°), and joint range of motion (>5°). No significant group-level rehabilitative changes were observed (all p > 0.05). In contrast, the assistive evaluation showed statistically significant increases in knee and hip range of motion across all walking conditions (p < 0.05), with all participants improving at the knee in every condition. Satisfaction scores (7-point scale) were high for size, appearance, usability, and set-up time (median ≥ 4/7), while weight, reliability, and timely performance received lower ratings (median 3.5/7). This exploratory study demonstrates a clear assistive biomechanical benefit of Agilik, particularly at the knee and hip. Individual-level analyses suggest that some participants may experience clinically meaningful improvements following training; however, these observations are hypothesis-generating and cannot be interpreted as evidence of a rehabilitative effect. Larger randomised controlled studies are needed to determine whether repeated exposure to assisted gait translates into sustained functional gains.
authors: Roberta Nossa; Giorgia Malerba; Anna Falivene; Eleonora Diella; Riccardo Riboni; Valentina Grasso; Luca Emanuele Molteni; Mattia Chiappini; Fabio Alexander Storm; Cristina Maghini; Emilia Biffi

title: Vibrotactile stimulation for upper-limb neurorehabilitation and sensorimotor training: a systematic review of clinical and mechanistic evidence.
abstract: Vibrotactile stimulation (VTS) has emerged as a potential sensory-based adjunct to upper limb rehabilitation by providing additional afferent feedback and supporting sensorimotor rehabilitation. This systematic review aimed to synthesize clinical evidence on VTS for post-stroke upper-limb rehabilitation and complementary mechanistic and technological evidence from healthy participants, with emphasis on intervention characteristics, stimulation parameters, clinical outcomes, neurophysiological effects, usability and safety. This review was conducted according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 guidelines and was retrospectively registered with the Open Science Framework. PubMed, PEDro, Web of Science and Google Scholar were searched for English-language full-text studies published between January 2015 and January 2026. Search terms included combinations of stroke, VTS, vibration, tactile, somatosensory, haptic, upper limb and hand. A total of 35 studies were included. Fourteen studies used direct upper-limb stimulation, six integrated VTS with robotic systems, two with virtual reality (VR), two with mirror visual feedback (MVF), seven with brain-computer interface (BCI) paradigms, and four with multimodal systems. Stimulation sites included the wrist, hand, fingers, fingertips, forearm, and upper arm, whereas reported frequencies, intensities, timing, and doses varied widely. Clinical studies suggested potential improvements in upper-limb motor function, sensory and proprioceptive function, spasticity, and affected-limb use, particularly when VTS accompanied active or task-oriented training. Mechanistic studies indicated that VTS may modulate sensorimotor rhythms, cortical activation, functional connectivity, and motor-imagery (MI)-related brain responses. Current evidence suggests that VTS may support upper-limb functional recovery after stroke. However, confidence in the evidence remains limited by small samples, heterogeneous protocols, and the frequent use of multimodal interventions that do not isolate the contribution of vibration. Further adequately powered randomized controlled trials are needed to determine clinical efficacy and to identify the stimulation parameters and feedback architectures most likely to benefit people after stroke.
authors: Wenbin Zhang; Kai Leng Catherine Chan; Hong Zeng; Baoguo Xu; Hexuan Hu; Minmin Miao; Aiguo Song; Ying Shen

title: A Comparison of Medial and Lateral Ligament Balance in Functional Versus Simulated Mechanical Alignment in Total Knee Arthroplasty Across CPAK Phenotypes: A Single-Center Study.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Despite the excellent long-term outcomes of total knee arthroplasty (TKA), up to 10% of patients remain dissatisfied. Robotic-assisted TKA enables individualized alignment strategies, such as functional alignment (FA). Proper alignment and soft tissue balance are considered key factors for positive clinical outcomes. This study compared medial and lateral ligament balance between simulated mechanical alignment (MA) and FA across different Coronal Plane Alignment of the Knee (CPAK) types using intraoperative robotic simulations. Methods: In this observational cohort study, 200 patients undergoing primary robotic-assisted TKA were included. Knee laxity was assessed intraoperatively under simulated MA and FA within the same knee. Laxity was defined as medial and lateral joint space opening under varus and valgus stress in flexion and extension. Balance was defined as an absolute difference of ≤2 mm. Outcomes were stratified by native CPAK phenotype in an exploratory subgroup analysis. Results: Functional alignment resulted in significantly improved ligament balance compared to simulated MA across CPAK types. The largest improvements were observed in CPAK type II, with the proportion of overall balanced knees increasing from 7.7% in simulated MA to 88.5% in FA. Improvements were observed in CPAK types II, V, VI and VIII and were mainly driven by a reduction in extension imbalance. Conclusions: Functional alignment leads to improved medial and lateral ligament balance compared to simulated MA. These findings suggest that the effect of the alignment strategy on soft tissue balance may differ according to the underlying knee phenotype.
authors: Anne Ruth van Meijeren; Daniëlle Langeloo; Hans-Peter van Jonbergen; Martin Stevens; Marrigje Floor Meijer

title: Medial expected gap (mEG): a quantitative, biology-guided predictor of coronal plane correction and knee balance in robotic functionally aligned total knee arthroplasty.
abstract: Osteophyte excision during total knee arthroplasty (TKA) influences gap balancing and deformity correction, but its effect on medial gap behavior remains poorly defined. This study evaluated the relationship between osteophyte burden, medial expected gap (mEG), and coronal correction in robotic assisted functional alignment TKA. This prospective study included 82 knees. Preoperative computed tomography images were used to measure medial tibial and femoral osteophytes. Following pilot development, mEG was calculated using an average osteophyte burden model with a non-linear physiological constraint capped at < 4 mm. Virtual gap balancing intentionally preserved the calculated mEG as medial tightness within predefined functional-alignment boundaries. Associations between osteophyte burden, mEG, coronal plane correction, and final knee balance were analyzed using correlation, regression, and group comparison statistics with bootstrap resampling for internal model validation. Raw medial osteophyte size demonstrated no significant association with lateral laxity severity (p = 0.357) or varus correctability (p = 0.302). Medial tibial (β = 0.12; p < 0.001) and medial femoral osteophytes (β = 0.16; p < 0.001) independently predicted mEG (R² = 0.47). Total osteophyte burden increased significantly across ascending mEG categories (p < 0.001), while final mEG values remained within a narrow physiological range. Mean coronal plane correction increased from 4.3° (mEG 1 mm) to 9.7° (mEG 4 mm) (p < 0.001). All knees achieved acceptable balance: 42 best balanced, 32 good, and 8 acceptable. Bootstrap internal validation supported the stability of the principal regression findings. The mEG provides a quantitative framework linking osteophyte burden to medial gap behavior, enabling preoperative planning of medial tightness and reproducible coronal correction during robotic assisted functional alignment TKA.Level of evidence: Level II, prospective cohort study.
authors: Harish Kumar Murugesan; Rex Chandrabose; T P Avinash; C Premanand

title: Objective Quantification of Soft-Tissue Balance in Total Knee Arthroplasty: Expanded Validation of the Pendulum Knee Drop Test Across Multiple Surgeons.
abstract: Despite increasing evidence showing major diversity in subjective balancing approaches, soft-tissue balance during total knee arthroplasty (TKA) remains primarily based upon empirical surgeon assessment. A quantitative technique for describing knee stiffness and laxity after TKA was previously introduced: the modified pendulum knee drop (PKD) test. This study expands upon prior validation work by evaluating the reproducibility of surgeon-directed balancing assessments compared with the modified PKD test across a larger cohort of arthroplasty surgeons. Robotic-assisted TKAs were performed on an advanced knee simulator model previously validated for ligament balancing investigations. After completing blinded polyethylene insert identification trials using manual balance assessments, eight high-volume arthroplasty surgeons underwent additional testing with the modified PKD test. During several testing cycles, polyethylene inserts ranging from 9 to 14 mm were randomly assigned and assessed. For both manual and PKD-assisted evaluations, accuracy, delta error, and intra- and interobserver reliability were computed. Stiffness and laxity behavior were described using oscillatory excursion measurements and logarithmic decrement values. Surgeons correctly identified polyethylene insert thickness manually in 60% of trials and within 1 mm in 84.2% of trials. In contrast, PKD-assisted balancing resulted in 97% correct insert identification (p < 0.001). The mean delta between surgeon-estimated and actual polyethylene thickness was 0.68 mm during manual assessment versus 0.05 mm with the PKD test (p < 0.001). Intraobserver reliability improved from a kappa of 0.61 during manual balancing to 0.96 with PKD assessment, while interobserver reliability improved from 0.38 to 0.97, respectively. The PKD test maintained highly reproducible thickness-independent stiffness ranking patterns across nearly all trials. High-volume arthroplasty surgeons demonstrated substantial variability during subjective soft-tissue balancing assessments, whereas the modified PKD test provided highly reproducible, objective biomechanical characterization of stiffness and laxity during TKA. These expanded findings further validate the PKD methodology as a reproducible tool to quantify soft-tissue knee laxity during robotic-assisted TKA.
authors: Kevin Abbruzzese; Michael A Mont; Michael Dunbar; Jared Weir; Chase W Smitterberg; Sally LiArno

title: Biomechanical Effect of Medial Collateral Ligament Repair With and Without Suture Augmentation on Knee Laxity and Anterior Cruciate Ligament Force.
abstract: The medial collateral ligament (MCL) is the most frequently injured knee ligament. MCL repair is a surgical technique intended to acutely reduce medial side laxity that can be performed in isolation or combined with suture augmentation (SA). To assess the effect of MCL repair with and without SA on (1) valgus laxity and anteromedial rotational laxity and (2) force carried by the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) and (3) to quantify load-sharing between the MCL repair and SA components. Controlled laboratory study. Seven cadaveric knees were tested using a 6 degrees of freedom robotic manipulator in 4 states: (1) intact, (2) MCL cut, (3) isolated MCL repair, and (4) MCL repair combined with SA. Valgus laxity and anteromedial rotational laxity were measured at 0°, 15°, 30°, and 90° of flexion. In situ ACL force and forces carried by the MCL repair components were assessed at peak valgus moment using principle of superposition. Valgus laxity after isolated MCL repair was greater than the intact state at all flexion angles >0° (P≤ .01). The addition of SA to MCL repair significantly reduced valgus laxity at 15° and 30° of flexion only (P≤ .02). Anteromedial rotational laxity after both MCL repairs was greater than the intact state at 90° of flexion (P < .01), whereas no differences were detected at 0° and 30°. For both MCL repairs, ACL force was less than in the MCL cut state and did not differ from the intact state. In situ forces carried by the repair and SA components did not differ for the MCL repair combined with SA. Both MCL repair with and without SA reduced ACL force relative to the MCL cut state. Addition of SA to MCL repair resulted in less residual valgus laxity but not less anteromedial rotational laxity. These findings suggest that MCL repair may reduce medial side laxity and partially offload the ACL relative to the MCL cut state. This is particularly important for treatment of combined ACL and MCL injuries, where the protection of the ACL graft or repair is most important immediately after surgery.
authors: Fidelius von Rehlingen-Prinz; David Z Shamritsky; Sebastian Rilk; Kyle N Kunze; Maximilian M Mueller; Bryce Demopoulos; Carl W Imhauser; Gregory S DiFelice
venue: The American journal of sports medicine

title: Impact of EMG-based interfaces for hand motor rehabilitation in stroke: A systematic review with evidence gap map and meta-analysis.
abstract: Electromyography (EMG)-based interventions have been proposed to improve hand/wrist motor recovery after stroke; however, their clinical value remains uncertain, as evidence for their effectiveness is inconsistent. This systematic review with meta-analysis evaluated the impact of different EMG-based rehabilitation approaches compared with non-EMG-based interventions in individuals with stroke. Seven databases were searched from inception to November 17, 2025, in accordance with PRISMA guidelines. Randomized controlled trials comparing EMG-based and non-EMG-based interventions for post-stroke hand or wrist rehabilitation were eligible. Interventions were classified into four categories: EMG-triggered electrical stimulation (EMG-ES), EMG-ES combined with other interventions, EMG-based robotic platforms, and EMG biofeedback combined with other interventions. Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 tool, and certainty of evidence was evaluated using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) approach. Meta-analyses were conducted for clinical outcomes classified according to the International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF) domains at post-intervention, follow-up <3 months, and follow-up ≥3 months. Thirty-eight studies involving 1,132 participants were included, of which 31 contributed to the meta-analyses. Eight studies were judged to have a low risk of bias, 13 to have some concerns, and 17 to have a high risk of bias. EMG-ES alone was not superior to conventional therapy. In contrast, EMG-ES combined with other interventions produced greater improvements across all ICF domains. EMG-based robotic platforms reduced wrist and finger spasticity, with effects sustained at long-term follow-up. EMG biofeedback primarily improved outcomes within the ICF body functions and structures domain. The effectiveness of EMG-based interventions depends on the rehabilitation strategy. EMG-ES, combined with other therapies, may be prioritized, whereas EMG-based robotic platforms may be useful in reducing spasticity. Further high-quality studies are needed to establish the clinical effectiveness of EMG-biofeedback approaches.
authors: Cristian D Guerrero-Mendez; Natanael Pereira Batista; José Osmar Alves Filho; Carina Marconi Germer; Leonardo Abdala Elias

title: Effect of Tibial Slope on Knee Mechanics for Posterior Cruciate Ligament Deficient Cruciate-retaining Total Knee Arthroplasty.
abstract: Debate continues over optimal tibial slope in cruciate-retaining versus cruciate-sacrificing total knee arthroplasty (TKA). Medial congruent tibial bearings, allow either posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) retention or sacrifice, further complicate decision-making-particularly when bone cuts have been completed for a cruciate-retainin (CR)-TKA and the PCL becomes compromised. This study evaluated the effect of tibial slope on knee mechanics in PCL-deficient CR-TKA using a medial congruent bearing. Fresh-frozen cadaveric knees underwent TKA with complete PCL resection and tested at tibial slopes of 0°, 3°, 5°, and 7° using robotic simulators. Passive laxity was assessed at 15°, 30°, 45°, 60°, and 90° of flexion using ±6 Nm internal-external torque, ±12 Nm varus-valgus torque, and ±100 N anterior-posterior and medial-lateral forces. Rapid-prototyped tibial bearings used to alter slope without additional bone cuts or rebalancing. Tibial slope had no significant effect (α = 0.05) on internal-external, varus-valgus, anterior-posterior, or medial-lateral laxity throughout flexion. Varus-valgus laxity decreased slightly with increasing slope, with a maximum difference of 1.4°. No consistent trend was observed in anterior posterior laxity. The joint shifted posteriorly on average of 2.2 mm per incremental slope increase. Lunge kinematics were not significantly affected. Increasing tibial slope did not significantly affect V/V laxity or knee kinematics after PCL compromise. While greater slope shifted the dwell point posteriorly, overall laxity remained unchanged. These findings suggest that recutting the tibia to adjust posterior tibial slope may not be necessary when PCL compromise occurs during CR-TKA using a medial congruent bearing design, provided appropriate soft tissue balance is maintained.
authors: Adrian Olson; Kyle Snethen; Eik Siggelkow; Marc Bandi; Craig Silverton; Nicholas B Frisch

title: Using Mobi-L RYMO to target spasticity in patient with chronic stroke: A case series study.
abstract: Stroke represents one of the main causes of permanent disability, with persistent upper limb motor deficits in 50% of patients; post-stroke spasticity limits functional recovery and quality of life. The aim of the study was to evaluate the effects of robotic device RYMO (Mobi-L) on spasticity management, motor function recovery, and subjective satisfaction in patients with chronic stroke. A descriptive case-series study was conducted on three patients with chronic stroke (>2 years). Each subject performed five sessions of robotic training with RYMO (Mobi-L) in active-assisted mode (45 minutes of effective training per session). Pre- and post-treatment assessments (T0-T1) included the Modified Ashworth Scale, Fugl-Meyer Assessment, Motricity Index, Barthel Index, Client Satisfaction Questionnaire and Patient Global Impression of Change. All patients completed the treatment cycle without adverse events, and showed a positive direction of change for MAS score at elbow and wrist districts. Motor improvements were more evident in proximal segments on FMA-UE, with slight increases of Motricity Index. Barthel Index remained unchanged, while satisfaction (CSQ-8) was high (31/32) and perceived change (PGIC) was moderate-positive (2/3). Despite the short duration of the protocol and the small sample size, results suggest a clinically impact on tone modulation and functional perception, with a higher self-perceived efficacy in daily activities.
authors: Emanuela Ricci; Riccardo Bettinardi; Sebastiano Rossi; Gianluca Ciardi
venue: Journal of stroke and cerebrovascular diseases : the official journal of National Stroke Association

title: Replication of the Robotic Evaluation of Articular Laxity (REAL) classification using intraoperative gap data in robot-assisted total knee arthroplasty.
abstract: Robot-assisted total knee arthroplasty (TKA) enables objective assessment of mediolateral (ML) balance; however, comparisons across cohorts remain difficult because "imbalance" has been poorly defined. The Robotic Evaluation of Articular Laxity (REAL) classification was proposed to standardize ML imbalance using a 3 × 3 framework, but independent replication of this novel classification has not been performed. We retrospectively reviewed 386 robot-assisted TKAs for osteoarthritis. Medial and lateral extension and flexion gaps were recorded before bone resection and at procedure end. ML imbalance was calculated as signed and absolute values. Primary outcomes were the distribution and normality of signed ML imbalance and the goodness-of-fit of varus REAL category frequencies versus the original REAL report using thresholds of 2.5 and 5.0 mm. Exploratory analyses evaluated patient-reported outcomes across initial REAL categories. In the full cohort, initial signed ML imbalance deviated from normality, whereas varus initial extension imbalance was nearly normal (1.08 ± 2.79 mm). Final absolute ML imbalance was about 1 mm in extension and 1.0-1.3 mm in flexion, with significant paired reductions in both (both p < 0.001). Varus REAL category frequencies differed from the original report, but deviations were modest and concentrated in a subset of cells. Patient-reported outcomes did not differ across initial REAL categories. In this independent robot-assisted TKA cohort, key features of the REAL framework were replicated in varus knees. Intraoperative balancing substantially improved ML balance, supporting the descriptive utility of REAL for organizing intraoperative balance phenotypes across cohorts.
authors: Yugo Morita; Nikolaos Mylonakis; Jonggu Shin; Mohammed El-Hassan; Ittai Shichman; Eustathios Kenanidis; Eleftherios Tsiridis; Peter K Sculco

title: The Efficacy of Proprioceptive Neuromuscular Facilitation-Based Robot-Assisted Therapy in Individuals With Stroke: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
abstract: The effects of combining robot-assisted therapy (RAT) with other physiotherapy approaches in stroke rehabilitation are of current interest. The aim of this study was to investigate the effect of proprioceptive neuromuscular facilitation (PNF)-based RAT on upper extremity (UE) motor performance, spasticity, activities of daily living (ADL), and quality of life (QoL) in individuals with stroke. Single-blind randomized controlled trial. Neurologic rehabilitation unit at a university. Thirty-nine individuals with stroke were enrolled in the study (RAT, n=20; Control group [CG], n=19). Both groups received 30 minutes of conventional rehabilitation per session; in addition, RAT completed 30 minutes of PNF and commonly used daily movement patterns with a robotic device, whereas CG performed the same exercises manually. All interventions were delivered 3 days per week for 8 weeks (60 min/session). Participants' UE performance was assessed using the Fugl-Meyer Upper Extremity Scale, Action Research Arm Test, Box and Block Test, and Nine-Hole Peg Test. Spasticity severity was assessed using the Modified Ashworth Scale, and ADL, QOL were assessed using ACTIVLIM, ABILHAND, Stroke Impact Scale (SIS). Mean age was 58.40±14.95 years in the RAT and 54.79±16.47 years in the CG. Fugl-Meyer Upper Extremity Scale, ACTIVLIM, ABILHAND, and SIS significantly increased in all groups after treatment (P<.05). At posttreatment, RAT showed significantly greater improvements than CG in Fugl-Meyer Upper Extremity Scale, Action Research Arm Test, Box and Block Test, Nine-Hole Peg Test, and muscle spasticity. In addition, decreases in wrist flexor and elbow flexor measurements were associated with 8.065- and 5.051-fold higher odds of being in the RAT, respectively. Conventional treatment combined with PNF-based RAT application has been shown to be more effective than traditional training in improving spasticity, motor performance, ADL, and QoL of patients with stroke.
authors: İzel Demirhan; Ender Ayvat; Fatma Ayvat; Özge Onursal; Özlem Navruz-Çelebi; Sibel Aksu-Yıldırım; Oğuzhan Kurşun; Muhammed Kılınç
venue: Archives of physical medicine and rehabilitation

title: Do Not Chase Symmetric Gaps: Native Asymmetry Linked to Better Recovery in Fixed-Deformity Total Knee Arthroplasty.
abstract:
Background

Non-correctable (fixed) knee deformities in total knee arthroplasty (TKA) are technically demanding, and the intraoperative factors driving recovery in this subgroup remain unclear. We hypothesized that, in non-correctable knees, a strategy that minimizes bone resection and preserves the patient's native medio-lateral laxity asymmetry, rather than chasing symmetric gaps through additional bone removal, would be associated with superior patient-reported functional outcomes at one year, whereas no such association would be observed in correctable knees.

Methods

We reviewed 861 consecutive primary robotic-arm-assisted TKAs (634 correctable, 227 non-correctable) at a single academic institution. Correctability was assessed intraoperatively by varus-valgus stress in extension: correctable if alignment came within 3° of neutral, non-correctable if it remained greater than 3° from neutral1-3. The robotic system quantified native and reconstructed compartment laxity in near extension (5 to 20°) and flexion (90 ± 10°) and recorded planned resection depths. Postoperative medial-lateral (M-L) laxity differential (reconstructed medial - lateral) was categorized as symmetric (less than 0.5 mm), partially corrected (0.5 to two mm), or preserved native asymmetry (two to five mm). The Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score for Joint Replacement (KOOS JR) and PROMIS (Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System) Physical Function were collected preoperatively and at six weeks, three months, and one year, stratified by correctability.

Results

The non-correctable knees showed greater PROMIS Physical Function improvement at three months (P = 0.003) and one year (7.0 ± 7.8 versus 4.9 ± 6.8; P = 0.036) despite similar preoperative scores. Among non-correctable knees, lower total bone resection volume was associated with greater KOOS JR improvement at one year (P = 0.016), strongest in the lateral flexion compartment (P = 0.039), indicating over-resection beyond implant thickness to achieve symmetric gaps is linked to poorer recovery. Greater postoperative flexion M-L laxity differential was also associated with greater KOOS JR (P = 0.009) and PROMIS (P = 0.044) improvement.

Conclusions

In non-correctable knees undergoing robotic-assisted TKA, preservation of native M-L laxity asymmetry is associated with superior patient-reported functional recovery. These findings challenge the universal goal of symmetric gaps and support an adaptive strategy that prioritizes bone preservation in fixed deformities.
authors: Suhardi VJ, Gwam C, DiGangi C, Hepinstall M, Rozell J, Meftah M.

title: Impact of EMG-based interfaces for hand motor rehabilitation in stroke: A systematic review with evidence gap map and meta-analysis.
abstract: Electromyography (EMG)-based interventions have been proposed to improve hand/wrist motor recovery after stroke; however, their clinical value remains uncertain, as evidence for their effectiveness is inconsistent. This systematic review with meta-analysis evaluated the impact of different EMG-based rehabilitation approaches compared with non-EMG-based interventions in individuals with stroke. Seven databases were searched from inception to November 17, 2025, in accordance with PRISMA guidelines. Randomized controlled trials comparing EMG-based and non-EMG-based interventions for post-stroke hand or wrist rehabilitation were eligible. Interventions were classified into four categories: EMG-triggered electrical stimulation (EMG-ES), EMG-ES combined with other interventions, EMG-based robotic platforms, and EMG biofeedback combined with other interventions. Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 tool, and certainty of evidence was evaluated using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) approach. Meta-analyses were conducted for clinical outcomes classified according to the International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF) domains at post-intervention, follow-up <3 months, and follow-up ≥3 months. Thirty-eight studies involving 1,132 participants were included, of which 31 contributed to the meta-analyses. Eight studies were judged to have a low risk of bias, 13 to have some concerns, and 17 to have a high risk of bias. EMG-ES alone was not superior to conventional therapy. In contrast, EMG-ES combined with other interventions produced greater improvements across all ICF domains. EMG biofeedback primarily improved outcomes within the ICF body functions and structures domain. The effectiveness of EMG-based interventions depends on the rehabilitation strategy. EMG-ES, combined with other therapies, may be prioritized, whereas EMG-based robotic platforms may be useful in reducing spasticity. Further high-quality studies are needed to establish the clinical effectiveness of EMG-biofeedback approaches.
authors: Guerrero-Mendez CD, Batista NP, Alves Filho JO, Germer CM, Elias LA.

title: Medial expected gap (mEG): a quantitative, biology-guided predictor of coronal plane correction and knee balance in robotic functionally aligned total knee arthroplasty.
abstract: Osteophyte excision during total knee arthroplasty (TKA) influences gap balancing and deformity correction, but its effect on medial gap behavior remains poorly defined. This study evaluated the relationship between osteophyte burden, medial expected gap (mEG), and coronal correction in robotic assisted functional alignment TKA. This prospective study included 82 knees. Preoperative computed tomography images were used to measure medial tibial and femoral osteophytes. Following pilot development, mEG was calculated using an average osteophyte burden model with a non-linear physiological constraint capped at < 4 mm. Virtual gap balancing intentionally preserved the calculated mEG as medial tightness within predefined functional-alignment boundaries. Associations between osteophyte burden, mEG, coronal plane correction, and final knee balance were analyzed using correlation, regression, and group comparison statistics with bootstrap resampling for internal model validation. Raw medial osteophyte size demonstrated no significant association with lateral laxity severity (p = 0.357) or varus correctability (p = 0.302). Medial tibial (β = 0.12; p < 0.001) and medial femoral osteophytes (β = 0.16; p < 0.001) independently predicted mEG (R² = 0.47). Total osteophyte burden increased significantly across ascending mEG categories (p < 0.001), while final mEG values remained within a narrow physiological range. Mean coronal plane correction increased from 4.3° (mEG 1 mm) to 9.7° (mEG 4 mm) (p < 0.001). All knees achieved acceptable balance: 42 best balanced, 32 good, and 8 acceptable. Bootstrap internal validation supported the stability of the principal regression findings. The mEG provides a quantitative framework linking osteophyte burden to medial gap behavior, enabling preoperative planning of medial tightness and reproducible coronal correction during robotic assisted functional alignment TKA.Level of evidence: Level II, prospective cohort study.
authors: Murugesan HK, Chandrabose R, Avinash TP, Premanand C.

title: Vibrotactile stimulation for upper-limb neurorehabilitation and sensorimotor training: a systematic review of clinical and mechanistic evidence.
abstract:
Background

Vibrotactile stimulation (VTS) has emerged as a potential sensory-based adjunct to upper limb rehabilitation by providing additional afferent feedback and supporting sensorimotor rehabilitation. This systematic review aimed to synthesize clinical evidence on VTS for post-stroke upper-limb rehabilitation and complementary mechanistic and technological evidence from healthy participants, with emphasis on intervention characteristics, stimulation parameters, clinical outcomes, neurophysiological effects, usability and safety.

Methods

This review was conducted according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 guidelines and was retrospectively registered with the Open Science Framework. PubMed, PEDro, Web of Science and Google Scholar were searched for English-language full-text studies published between January 2015 and January 2026. Search terms included combinations of stroke, VTS, vibration, tactile, somatosensory, haptic, upper limb and hand.

Results

A total of 35 studies were included. Fourteen studies used direct upper-limb stimulation, six integrated VTS with robotic systems, two with virtual reality (VR), two with mirror visual feedback (MVF), seven with brain-computer interface (BCI) paradigms, and four with multimodal systems. Stimulation sites included the wrist, hand, fingers, fingertips, forearm, and upper arm, whereas reported frequencies, intensities, timing, and doses varied widely. Clinical studies suggested potential improvements in upper-limb motor function, sensory and proprioceptive function, spasticity, and affected-limb use, particularly when VTS accompanied active or task-oriented training. Mechanistic studies indicated that VTS may modulate sensorimotor rhythms, cortical activation, functional connectivity, and motor-imagery (MI)-related brain responses.

Conclusion

Current evidence suggests that VTS may support upper-limb functional recovery after stroke. However, confidence in the evidence remains limited by small samples, heterogeneous protocols, and the frequent use of multimodal interventions that do not isolate the contribution of vibration. Further adequately powered randomized controlled trials are needed to determine clinical efficacy and to identify the stimulation parameters and feedback architectures most likely to benefit people after stroke.
authors: Zhang W, Catherine Chan KL, Zeng H, Xu B, Hu H, Miao M, Song A, Shen Y.

title: Evaluating the rehabilitative and assistive impact of the Agilik exoskeleton: a pre-post single-group study in children with cerebral palsy.
abstract:
Introduction

Cerebral palsy (CP) is a common childhood-onset neurological condition often associated with crouch gait, a pathological walking pattern impairing mobility. Wearable robotic devices are emerging as promising tools for paediatric gait rehabilitation, but evidence on their rehabilitative and assistive effects remains limited. This exploratory study evaluated the rehabilitative and assistive effects of a 10-session training programme using Agilik, a paediatric knee exoskeleton, in children with CP and crouch gait, during level-ground, uphill, and downhill walking.

Methods

Eight children with CP completed the intervention. Assessments were performed at baseline (T0) and post-intervention (T1), including walking endurance, speed, balance, spasticity, and clinical joint and muscle length assessments. Three-dimensional gait analysis (GRAIL system) quantified sagittal-plane hip, knee, and ankle range of motion during level-ground, uphill, and downhill walking. At T1, joint range of motion was analysed with and without Agilik to assess its assistive effect. User satisfaction was evaluated using the child-adapted QUEST 2.1 questionnaire.

Results

Given the exploratory nature of this study, results were interpreted primarily at the individual level using predefined minimal clinically important difference (MCID) thresholds. When clinically relevant changes occurred, improvements were more frequently observed than deteriorations in walking endurance (MCID > 15 m), speed (MCID > 0.1 m/s), muscle lengths (>5°), and joint range of motion (>5°). No significant group-level rehabilitative changes were observed (all p > 0.05). In contrast, the assistive evaluation showed statistically significant increases in knee and hip range of motion across all walking conditions (p < 0.05), with all participants improving at the knee in every condition. Satisfaction scores (7-point scale) were high for size, appearance, usability, and set-up time (median ≥ 4/7), while weight, reliability, and timely performance received lower ratings (median 3.5/7).

Conclusions

This exploratory study demonstrates a clear assistive biomechanical benefit of Agilik, particularly at the knee and hip. Individual-level analyses suggest that some participants may experience clinically meaningful improvements following training; however, these observations are hypothesis-generating and cannot be interpreted as evidence of a rehabilitative effect. Larger randomised controlled studies are needed to determine whether repeated exposure to assisted gait translates into sustained functional gains.
authors: Nossa R, Malerba G, Falivene A, Diella E, Riboni R, Grasso V, Molteni LE, Chiappini M, Storm FA, Maghini C, Biffi E.

title: Penjadwalan Proses Dinamis Berbasis Kombinasi Deadline dan LLF pada MES SmartEdu Station
abstract: Penjadwalan proses pada lingkungan manufaktur dinamis memerlukan mekanisme pengambilan keputusan yang mampu merespons perubahan kondisi produksi secara cepat dan tepat. Penelitian ini bertujuan mengimplementasikan metode Deadline Scheduling dan Least Laxity First (LLF) pada Manufacturing Execution System (MES) SmartEdu Station untuk mendukung penjadwalan proses dinamis pada lingkungan job shop manufacturing. Penelitian dilakukan melalui pengembangan modul penjadwalan yang mengintegrasikan evaluasi deadline dan perhitungan nilai laxity dalam proses penentuan prioritas pekerjaan. Data penelitian berupa beberapa pekerjaan produksi dengan waktu kedatangan, waktu proses, dan batas penyelesaian yang berbeda. Hasil penelitian menunjukkan bahwa metode Deadline Scheduling mampu mengidentifikasi kelayakan pekerjaan berdasarkan batas waktu penyelesaian, sedangkan metode LLF mampu menentukan prioritas pekerjaan secara dinamis berdasarkan tingkat urgensi yang direpresentasikan oleh nilai laxity. Implementasi kedua metode menghasilkan mekanisme penjadwalan yang adaptif terhadap perubahan kondisi produksi dan mampu mendukung pengambilan keputusan produksi secara lebih efektif pada MES SmartEdu Station.
authors: Yuliadi Erdani; Setyawan Ajie Sukarno; Muhammad Giri Suhada; Susetyo Bagas Bhaskoro; Ismail Rokhim

title: Evolución del diseño mecánico de un robot de rehabilitación en entorno acuático
abstract: Neurological disorders, such as stroke, multiple sclerosis, or severe neuropathies, drastically impact patient autonomy and quality of life. Although rehabilitation technologies have demonstrated great potential, their application remains limited in patients with severe impairments, particularly those presenting high levels of spasticity. In this context, aquatic therapy stands out for its capacity to reduce such spasticity through the physical properties of water, which facilitate movement and promote muscle relaxation. Under this premise, the MIRRA project emerged, an innovative initiative that combines robotic technologies with the benefits of the aquatic environment. This paper presents the evolution in the mechanical design of a new robotic system specifically conceived for hand rehabilitation in subaquatic environments, describing its development and improvements relative to its previous stages.
authors: Fco. Javier Miñano; Daniel Diaz-Diaz; Javier Chinchilla-Pastor; Yolanda Vales; Andrea Blanco; Nicolas Garcia-Aracil

title: Research progress of upper limb rehabilitation robots
abstract: Stroke, the leading cause of adult disability globally, results in ~2 million annual new cases in China, with 55% – 75% of patients experiencing persistent upper limb motor dysfunction 3 months post-treatment. Traditional one-on-one manual rehabilitation has three critical limitations: (1) low training efficiency due to therapist resource constraints and high workload; (2) lack of precise force control during complex phases (e.g., flaccid paralysis, spasticity); (3) absence of real-time rehabilitation parameter measurement, relying on subjective clinical experience without data support. As interdisciplinary medical-engineering innovations, upper limb rehabilitation robots provide precise repetitive training to promote neuroplasticity, addressing rehabilitation resource shortages. This paper systematically reviews their research progress: analyzing upper limb physiological structure and rehabilitation requirements; classifying robots by interaction mode (end-effector/exoskeleton) and drive form, elaborating structural characteristics and application scenarios; summarizing control strategies and assessment standards; and analyzing current challenges and future trends. Research indicates flexible exoskeletons, AI-assisted control, and multimodal sensor fusion will be key directions, enabling more natural, personalized, and efficient rehabilitation.
authors: Hu Liu; Jinhai Wan; Xudong Zeng; Long Huang

title: Inspect Robots: Evaluating the Capabilities and Safety of Embodied AI
abstract: General purpose language models are increasingly able to control robotic hardware. Understanding the capabilities and safety of these models when embodied is therefore increasingly important for understanding their societal impact and risks. To this end, we introduce Inspect Robots, a modular, open-source framework for developing and running evaluations of embodied agents. Inspect Robots pairs customizable, reusable abstractions for specifying physical evaluations and analyzing their results with infrastructure that automates evaluation setup, execution and termination. We demonstrate Inspect Robots by using it to evaluate the capabilities and safety of six policies based on frontier language models. Inspect Robots has seen significant early uptake, receiving nearly 100,000 downloads in the three months since its release.
authors: Christopher Leet; Achu Menon; Sravanthi Machcha; Sabrina Zou; Aayushya Patel; Aditya Kumar Singh; Anish Kr Singh; Galaba Vamsi; Javin Ahuja; Sai Asish Yamani; Tushar Anand; Vedang Alle; Zihan Zhang; Tzu Kit Chan; Jay Chooi

title: Rediseño y validación de un encapsulado estanco para un nuevo actuador híbrido subacuático
abstract: Injuries to the central nervous system, such as strokes, have a significant impact on people’s independence, as they cause motor disorders such as spasticity, thereby limiting and affecting the quality of life of those affected. In recent years, work has been carried out on the NOHA project, investigating a new paradigm of robotic-aquatic rehabilitation that combines traditional robotics with the benefits of hydrotherapy. In the latest tests carried out, certain issues were identified regarding the watertightness of the manufactured enclosure, which this article aims to resolve. The results of the redesign and validation of the new version is presented below, suggesting improved performance in terms of watertightness and the efficiency of the PID positional control.
authors: Javier Chinchilla-Pastor; Manuel Herraiz-Sala; Fco. Javier Miñano; Julián Girona-Mora; Andrea Blanco; Nicolas Garcia-Aracil

title: From Underuse to Recovery: Intensive Neurorehabilitation of Deforming Spastic Paresis in Resource-Contrasted Settings - A Unified Physiopathological Framework
abstract: Background: Deforming spastic paresis following stroke remains one of the most disabling sequelae of upper motor neuron injury. The pathophysiological cascade - from neural lesion to spastic myopathy through progressive underuse -is well characterised but systematically under-treated, particularly in resource-limited settings where conventional physiotherapy remains sparse and low-intensity. The concept of therapeutic intensity, formalised through the formula I=(R×L×E)/T (repetitions × load × effort / time), provides a pharmacological-like framework for dosing neurorehabilitation. This paper presents a unified physiopathological model of underuse-driven spastic paresis and its reversal through intensive, task-oriented physical therapy, illustrated by two clinical cases treated in contrasted resource environments.Methods: Two male patients (58 and 52 years) with chronic post-stroke hemiparesis (14 and 22 months post-onset respectively) underwent a 12-week intensive neurorehabilitation protocol combining aggressive prolonged stretching, maximum-amplitude alternating movements, a guided self-rehabilitation contract (CAG), and - in the Cameroonian case -the Cogni-Famille task-shifting protocol engaging trained family members. Case 1 was treated at the private physiotherapy practice in Vitry-sur-Seine, France; Case 2 at the Regional Hospital of Bafoussam, Cameroon.Results: Both patients demonstrated clinically significant functional recovery across all measured domains. The Modified Ashworth Scale (wrist flexors) decreased from 3/4 to 1+/4 (Case 1) and from 3/4 to 2/4 (Case 2) at 12 weeks. The E5E retraction index decreased from 0.62 to 0.31 and from 0.74 to 0.41, respectively. Walking perimeter increased from 300 m to 1,800 m (Case 1) and from 80 m to 1,200 m (Case 2). Therapeutic intensity, measured by I=(R×L×E)/T, increased 6-fold in Case 1 and 17-fold in Case 2 relative to prior conventional treatment. Both patients achieved their primary functional goals: partial return to professional activity (France) and full return to farming (Cameroon).Conclusion: Intensive neurorehabilitation - applied consistently, regardless of resource context -can reverse the underuse-driven pathological cascade and achieve functional recovery well beyond conventional expectations. The therapeutic intensity formula operationalises dosing in a replicable, measurable manner. The Low-Tech, High-Sense paradigm demonstrates that human expertise, not technological equipment, is the primary determinant of neuroplastic recovery in post-stroke spastic paresis.
authors: Ibrahim Npochinto Moumeni; Abdel-Nasser Njikam Moumeni; Bakary Coulibaly; Mohamed Lamine Moumeni; Bristher Horlisther Tchuidjio Ketchogué; Yacouba Njankouo Mapoure

Graphical abstract The graphical abstract summarizes the findings of a systematic review and meta-analysis including 38 studies and 1,132 participants. title: Neurorehabilitation for cognitive and motor recovery: mechanisms, interventions, and translational advances
abstract: This narrative review synthesizes recent advances in neurorehabilitation, focusing on mechanisms of neural plasticity, glial cell function, and interventions for cognitive and motor recovery. We explore multidisciplinary approaches, including cognitive training, motor rehabilitation, neurostimulation, and regenerative therapies, highlighting their translational potential. Special attention is given to clinically relevant rehabilitation modifiers and complications, including spasticity, frailty, and post-stroke epilepsy, alongside strategies for enhancing quality of life and social reintegration. Emerging technologies such as brain-computer interfaces, virtual reality, and robotics are discussed for their role in personalized rehabilitation. This review emphasizes evidence-based, patient-centered interventions to enhance functional recovery and quality of life, identifying future directions for personalized neurorehabilitation across stroke survivors, elderly, and frail populations.
authors: Yingchao Guan; Yanan Gao

title: Effects of robot-assisted gait training on walking capacity and gross motor function in children with central nervous system impairments: a systematic review and meta-analysis predominantly based on cerebral palsy studies
abstract: Abstract Background Children with cerebral palsy (CP) and other central nervous system (CNS) impairments often have limitations in walking capacity and gross motor function. Robot-assisted gait training (RAGT) is increasingly used in pediatric rehabilitation, but existing evidence remains inconsistent. Objective To evaluate the effects of RAGT versus conventional therapy for improving walking capacity and broader motor and functional outcomes in children with CP and other CNS impairments. Methods PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, the Cochrane Library, CINAHL, and ClinicalTrials.gov were searched from inception to April 1, 2026. Randomized controlled trials of children aged 2–18 years with CP or other CNS impairments were included. Risk of bias and methodological quality were assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 tool and PEDro scale. Random-effects meta-analyses used mean differences (MDs) or standardized mean differences (SMDs), and certainty of evidence was assessed using GRADE. Results A total of 22 studies ( n = 718) were included, of which 20 focused on CP and two on spinal cord injury (SCI); no studies involving acquired brain injury (ABI) were identified. Compared with conventional therapy, RAGT was associated with greater improvements in walking speed (SMD = 0.58, 95% CI 0.18 to 0.98; P = 0.005; GRADE: high) and 6-minute walk distance (6MWD) (MD = 38.68 m, 95% CI 22.61 to 54.75; P < 0.00001; GRADE: high). An exploratory analysis of two studies also suggested a reduction in the Physiological cost index. No significant differences were observed for GMFM-88, balance, spasticity, or functional independence. Exploratory subgroup analyses suggested larger effects on walking speed with interventions ≥ 8 weeks and identified a significant subgroup difference by robot type for 6MWD, but not for walking speed. Conclusion RAGT may improve walking speed and endurance in children with CP. Insufficient evidence exists for other pediatric CNS impairments, precluding definitive conclusions for children with SCI or ABI. Preliminary subgroup analyses indicate intervention duration and robotic device type may moderate therapeutic benefits, but require further validation. Additional high-quality trials adopting uniform outcome measures are warranted to assess a wider range of functional endpoints and delineate RAGT’s efficacy across pediatric CNS conditions other than CP.
authors: Xiao Wu; Xin Li; Jüping Liang; ZhengQuan Chen; Jun Zhang; XiaoYan Yang; Qimeng Fan; Haibin Guo; LiHong Liao; Qing Du

title: Gait disorders in neurological diseases: clinical significance, assessment methods, and rehabilitation potential
abstract: Gait disturbances are a common manifestation of neurological disorders and a major contributor to functional limitations, increased fall risk, and reduced quality of life. Nevertheless, gait impairment often remains underrecognized in routine neurological practice, and its evaluation is frequently confined to basic spatiotemporal parameters, such as gait speed, without sufficient consideration of the underlying pathophysiological mechanisms. The aim of this review was to summarize current evidence regarding the types and mechanisms of gait disorders in neurological diseases, clinical approaches to gait pattern analysis, and contemporary therapeutic strategies. A literature search was conducted in PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, EMBASE, and The Cochrane Library, focusing on studies examining the clinical characteristics of pathological gait, methods of gait assessment, rehabilitation interventions, and medication-based management of gait disturbances in patients with neurological conditions. The available evidence indicates that different neurological pathologies can result in comparable alterations in fundamental gait parameters, including decreased walking speed and reduced step length. However, detailed gait pattern analysis enables determination of the specific locomotor pattern and facilitates identification of the predominant mechanisms underlying gait impairment, including muscle weakness, spasticity, sensory deficits, impaired motor control, limited joint mobility, and pain. Furthermore, distinguishing primary gait abnormalities from compensatory adaptations is essential for selecting targeted and effective interventions. Optimal functional outcomes are achieved through comprehensive, mechanism-oriented approaches that integrate physical therapy, orthotic management, and oral medication-based or injection-based therapies.
authors: Yuriy Flomin; Anastasiia L. Orlovska; A.V. Tsyhanii; M.V. Guliaieva; Mykola Romanyshyn; Anastasiia Honchar; Iryna R. Havryliv; Maksym H. Tsariapkin

title: Assist and resist: a dual-track framework for pediatric exoskeleton rehabilitation
abstract: Wearable exoskeletons have usually entered pediatric rehabilitation through a familiar promise: to assist movement that disease, weakness, or poor motor control has made difficult. This logic is clinically intuitive. For children with neuromotor disorders, robotic assistance may help them stand, step, practice gait, or experience movements otherwise unavailable to them. Yet a recent Nature study by Li and colleagues (1) raises a different question for pediatric rehabilitation: what if the next generation of pediatric exoskeletons should not only assist movement, but also safely resist it? This question matters because pediatric rehabilitation occurs during growth. Children with neuromuscular disease, cerebral palsy (CP), developmental delay, and related neuromotor disorders are not simply smaller adults undergoing functional recovery. They are developing musculoskeletal systems, motor strategies, neural pathways, and participation habits while disease-related weakness, disuse, spasticity, fatigue, or impaired motor control may narrow their future functional reserve. The clinical objective is therefore not only to improve today's movement, but also to protect or redirect tomorrow's developmental trajectory. Li et al. studied a lightweight, portable, isokinetic resistance robot in six juveniles with spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) type II (1). The findings are preliminary and do not establish general efficacy across pediatric neuromotor disorders. Nevertheless, they may represent a starting whistle from China for a wider debate: pediatric exoskeleton rehabilitation should not be limited to assistance toward normative movement. In selected children, the more important therapeutic stimulus may be individually dosed effort, progressive resistance, and neuromuscular adaptation.Most lower-limb exoskeletons in research and development are designed to reduce effort. This may be appropriate when the goal is immediate mobility, energy conservation, or compensatory access to standing and walking. Wearable lower-limb exoskeletons have increasingly been explored for gait training and mobility support across neuromuscular impairments (2). In pediatric SMA, previous work with the ATLAS 2030 gait exoskeleton suggested that robotic gait assistance may improve selected strength and range-of-motion outcomes, but such devices remain primarily assistive rather than resistive in therapeutic logic (3). Reduced effort, however, is not always synonymous with rehabilitation. If the target is muscle growth, strength, motor-unit recruitment, or longer-term functional carryover after device removal, a device that makes movement easier may deliver an incomplete training signal. The Nature study is important because it reverses this conventional logic. Li et al. designed a 0.96 kg wearable knee robot that provided isokinetic resistance training for children with SMA type II (1). Isokinetic resistance is conceptually appealing because it regulates movement velocity while allowing resistance to adapt to the user's output. In contrast to fixed external loads, which may be too difficult or unsafe for weak children, controlled isokinetic resistance can maintain effort across a usable range of motion while limiting abrupt overload (4). This approach addresses a major translational gap. Traditional isokinetic systems are bulky, expensive, institution-based, and often developed for sports rehabilitation or adult strength assessment rather than for children with severe weakness. Portable robotics may therefore create a missing middle ground between conventional physiotherapy and laboratory-grade dynamometry: a way to deliver measurable, progressive, and individualized strengthening stimulus in the home. The outcomes reported by Li et al. were notable not merely because function improved, but because several levels of adaptation moved in the same direction. After six weeks of high-intensity isokinetic training, participants improved sit-to-stand performance, peak knee extension torque, range of motion, work per extension, quadriceps cross-sectional and volume measures, physiological cross-sectional area, and femoral nerve compound muscle action potential (1). These convergent functional, muscular, and neurophysiological signals suggest that the robot may have acted not as a temporary mobility aid, but as a training interface capable of inducing biological adaptation. Figure 1 summarizes this proposed shift from assistance-centered to adaptationcentered pediatric exoskeleton rehabilitation.The pediatric context changes the value of resistance training. In adults, resistance exercise is often discussed as a way to restore or preserve function. In children with neuromotor disorders, it may also influence the developmental accumulation of strength, muscle size, joint control, and task confidence (5). A small gain during a critical period may alter what activities a child can practice, which in turn may alter subsequent motor learning and participation. This point aligns with recent evidence from CP rehabilitation. In our recent review, resistance training showed favorable effects on proxy indicators of muscle fiber diameter in ambulatory children with CP, whereas evidence for power training was less consistent for hypertrophy-related outcomes (6). However, most available evidence concerns ambulatory children with lower disability levels, leaving the optimal protocol for children with greater functional disability unresolved (6). The Nature study should be read against this unresolved problem. Children who most need muscle development may be least able to perform conventional strengthening with adequate dose, load progression, safety, and adherence. Portable resistive exoskeletons could help solve this paradox. They may allow a weak child to train within a narrow but therapeutically meaningful zone: difficult enough to recruit muscle and stimulate adaptation, but controlled enough to avoid unsafe loading, compensatory movement, or excessive fatigue. This is especially relevant when growth itself is not sufficient to offset diseaserelated weakness or disuse. In SMA, natural history studies have shown limited or declining motor trajectories in many affected children, despite modern supportive care (7,8). In CP, impaired muscle morphology and reduced muscle volume are closely tied to weakness, reduced joint power, gait limitation, and long-term musculoskeletal complications (9,10). The growth window is therefore not simply a background variable; it is the clinical window in which rehabilitation dose may matter most. In typically developing children, muscle morphology and strength change measurably over months of growth (11). In contrast, children with SMA may show relative stability or decline in thigh muscle volume and function over comparable developmental periods, depending on disease type, severity, and treatment context (12). Against this background, the rapid quadriceps morphological changes reported by Li et al. after six weeks of robot-mediated isokinetic training (1) are difficult to dismiss as ordinary growth alone. 4. Beyond SMA: promise, but not one-size-fits-all The most immediate interpretation of Li et al. concerns SMA type II. In that population, pharmacological advances have changed survival and disease trajectories (13), but motor rehabilitation remains necessary because medication does not fully normalize muscle, nerve, or functional development (14). Exercise and strengthening have been explored in SMA, with some promising findings but also mixed results and practical barriers (15,16). More recently, neuromodulatory approaches, including non-invasive spinal cord stimulation in children with SMA and epidural spinal cord stimulation in individuals with SMA, have expanded the therapeutic landscape (17,18). Yet these approaches also reinforce a central principle: biological modulation is unlikely to replace active motor training. A portable isokinetic robot may therefore offer a more precise way to test whether high-activation resistance training can complement pharmacological, neuromodulatory, and conventional rehabilitation strategies. The broader implication is not that all pediatric neuromotor disorders should receive the same resistive exoskeleton protocol. Rather, the platform invites diagnosis-specific testing. Candidate populations may include children with SMA type II or III, ambulatory and selected nonambulatory children with CP who have marked antigravity weakness, children with developmental delay and low postural or lower-limb strength, selected congenital myopathies or neuropathies, and children recovering from prolonged immobilization or pediatric critical illness. In each case, the central question would differ: preserving motor units in SMA, improving muscle morphology and joint power in CP, increasing antigravity strength in developmental delay, or rebuilding functional reserve after immobilization. Caution is equally important. Progressive neuromuscular diseases are heterogeneous. In muscular dystrophies and some myopathies, resistance intensity, eccentric stress, fatigue accumulation, and muscle damage require careful evaluation. In children with spasticity or dystonia, poorly controlled resistance may reinforce abnormal movement strategies or increase discomfort. In children with cardiopulmonary compromise, scoliosis, contractures, fragile bones, or severe fatigue, resistance training requires additional safeguards. Thus, the starting whistle should not trigger indiscriminate adoption. It should trigger systematic pediatric trials designed around disease mechanism, developmental stage, and safety phenotype.The portability of the device is not a minor engineering feature. In pediatric rehabilitation, dose is often limited by transportation, clinic availability, caregiver time, cost, and child engagement (19,20). Home-compatible devices could substantially change the achievable dose of resistance training. They could also turn rehabilitation from episodic clinic attendance into a more continuous developmental intervention.Three features are particularly important. First, adjustable resistance may allow progression as the child improves, avoiding the common problem that a fixed exercise becomes either too hard at baseline or too easy after adaptation. Second, embedded sensing can quantify torque, angle, velocity, range of motion, adherence, and fatigue-related decline, making home rehabilitation more measurable than many conventional exercise programs. Third, gamified feedback may improve motivation, especially when training is repetitive or demanding. However, home use also shifts responsibility. Caregivers may become co-therapists, raising questions about training burden, supervision quality, adverse-event recognition, and equity. A device that works in a well-supported research setting may not work similarly in families with limited time, income, digital literacy, or access to clinical backup. Future pediatric exoskeleton trials should therefore evaluate not only efficacy, but also implementation: who can use the device safely, how much caregiver training is required, what monitoring is necessary, and whether benefits are distributed fairly.The Nature study should not be interpreted as definitive evidence that resistive exoskeletons are effective for pediatric neuromotor rehabilitation across diagnoses. The sample was small, the target disease was rare, no randomized control group was included, and the prototype focused on concentric isokinetic knee extension (1). These limitations are understandable in an early study of a rare pediatric condition, but they define the next research agenda. The next step is not simply to test whether resistive exoskeletons "work," but to determine for whom, under what loading conditions, and with what safeguards during growth. First, larger multicenter trials are needed, particularly in rare diseases where single-center samples will remain small. Designs may include randomized crossover trials, delayed-start controls, or adaptive protocols that balance rigor with ethical concerns about withholding promising rehabilitation. Second, outcomes should be developmentally anchored. Pediatric trials should track not only short-term torque or task performance, but also growth-adjusted muscle morphology, motor milestones, participation, fatigue, pain, falls, caregiver burden, and long-term retention after device withdrawal. Third, dosing studies are essential. The field needs to know how intensity, velocity, session frequency, total repetitions, stiffness, and rest intervals interact with age, diagnosis, fatigue, and growth. Fourth, assistive and resistive modes should be compared and combined. Some children may need assistance to access movement practice and resistance to stimulate adaptation. The clinical art may lie not in choosing "assist" or "resist," but in sequencing both. Finally, safety must be treated as a developmental construct. A safe device is not only one that avoids immediate injury. It is one that does not increase maladaptive compensation, pain, fatigue, fear, inequity, or caregiver overload over months and years. Pediatric wearable robotics must therefore move beyond engineering feasibility toward longitudinal developmental rehabilitation science. The assist-versus-resist decision, together with the safeguards needed for pediatric translation, is summarized in Figure 1. The starting whistle from China should be heard clearly, but not prematurely celebrated as the final score. Its message is more important than any single outcome: pediatric exoskeletons may become more than devices that help children move while they are worn. If designed around individualized resistance, measurable dose, home feasibility, and disease-specific safety, they may become platforms for neuromuscular development during the years when development matters most.
authors: Hua Xia; Xia Liu; Bo Liu; Yang Zhang

title: Electrotherapy in Pediatric Rehabilitation: A Structured Narrative Review of Clinical Applications, Treatment Parameters, Safety, and Evidence Gaps
abstract: Background/Objectives: Electrotherapy encompasses diverse therapeutic modalities used in Physical and Rehabilitation Medicine, but pediatric evidence varies substantially across modality–indication pairs. This structured narrative review critically synthesized evidence on clinical applications, treatment parameters, efficacy, safety, and evidence gaps in pediatric rehabilitation. Methods: PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched for publications from 1 January 2000 to 17 July 2026. Evidence was synthesized by electrotherapy modality and clinical indication and classified using Oxford Centre for Evidence-Based Medicine (OCEBM) Levels of Evidence. Results: The strongest evidence was identified for rESWT in cerebral palsy-related spasticity; TENS and IFC in bladder and bowel dysfunction; and NMES/FES, rTMS, and tDCS for selected motor rehabilitation outcomes. PBM/LLLT, PEMF, and HILT showed promising but indication-specific evidence, whereas TECAR had preliminary adjunctive evidence. Therapeutic ultrasound and Deep Oscillation Therapy remain insufficiently supported, and several modalities lack pediatric clinical evidence. Short-term tolerability was generally favorable, but long-term safety data remain limited. Conclusions: Electrotherapy has an adjunctive role in selected pediatric rehabilitation indications, but prescription should be based on specific modality–indication pairs. Standardized multicenter trials and long-term safety studies are required.
authors: Andreea Veronica Stavăr; Cristina Octaviana Daia; Brînduşa Ilinca Mitoiu; Madalina Codruta Verenca

title: Does size matter? A secondary analysis of the effect of region-of-interest size on muscle echotexture features of the gastrocnemius medialis in stroke
abstract: The analysis of muscle echotexture using ultrasound imaging is attracting increasing interest for assessing muscle tissue across different health conditions. However, variability in the size of the region of interest (ROI) can affect echotexture assessment. This study examines how varying ROI sizes may impact the quantification of echotexture in the gastrocnemius medialis of post-stroke individuals. A secondary analysis was performed on 130 ultrasound images from 22 post-stroke individuals. We extracted 21 echotexture features, including echovariation (EV) and mean echointensity (EI), from five ROI sizes: whole-muscle (maximum muscle tissue area), 300 × 300, 200 × 200, 100 × 100, and 50 × 50 pixels. Friedman tests, Bland-Altman analyses, and linear regression models were employed to evaluate the influence of ROI size on feature variability and measurement agreement. EV values decreased significantly as ROI size decreased ( p < 0.001), whereas EI showed the opposite trend, increasing significantly with progressively smaller ROIs. Results for the remaining features were more heterogeneous, although variability generally increased as ROI size decreased. The 300 × 300-pixel ROI showed the highest agreement with the whole-muscle ROI, minimizing variability while minimizing the inclusion of non-muscular structures. ROI size substantially influences quantitative echotexture measurements, particularly EV and EI values. As ROI size decreased, greater variability and lower agreement with the original whole-muscle ROI approach were observed. These findings highlight the methodological importance of ROI selection and delineation in quantitative muscle ultrasound research and may facilitate more consistent interpretation and potential clinical translation. Analysis of the Correlation Between Ultrasound Imaging and Functional Parameters in the Medial Gastrocnemius Muscle in Post-stroke Patients With Spasticity in the Lower Limb (US-function), https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06411587, NCT06411587, 2024-05-07.
authors: Diego Lapuente‐Hernández; Borhan Asadi; Alberto Carcasona-Otal; Clara Pujol; Pablo Herrero; Elżbieta Skorupska

title: Lihasaktivaatio ja voiman kontrolli CP-vammaisilla lapsilla
abstract: Cerebral palsy (CP) is the most common physical disability in children and adolescents in devel-oped countries, with a prevalence of approximately 0.2–0.3% of the population. CP is a result of brain damage or brain development disorders during the fetal stage and early childhood. There is no cure for the disability, but the motor symptoms, such as reduced muscle strength and spasticity, can be alleviated with physiotherapy, foot-ankle orthoses, and surgery. The purpose of this study was to examine the neuromuscular control of muscle force production and its connection to walking ability. The study investigated the muscle activation, maximal force production, force control of the gastrocnemius medialis muscle (GM) in children with CP and in a control group of typically developed (TD) children. Additionally, it was determined whether these results correlated with the walking ability (walking speed and walking energy consumption) of the CP group. The children were aged 9–18 years, and the CP group's GMFCS classifications were 1 or 2. The measurements were conducted in 2024 by Maxwell Thurston and his research group. In the study, force production control was measured with a dynamometer test where the subjects had to steadily increase force and hold it for ten seconds at a 50 % level of maximal force production. At the same time, a high-density surface electromyography (HDsEMG) grid was placed over the GM muscle to measure muscle activation. Measurement results were analyzed using MATLAB scripts. The variables obtained from the results were spatial entropy, maximal voluntary contraction (MVC), normalized average deviation from target force level, and normalized force standard deviation. The MVC of the GM muscle was significantly higher in the control group, as expected. Spatial entropy and normalized average deviation of force were slightly higher in the CP group. Normalized standard deviation, however, was higher in the control group, which was contrary to the hypothesis. Statistical power of the results, except MVC, was poor. No clear correlation with walking ability was found, except for a moderate negative correlation between energy consumption and normalized average deviation. The results were likely affected by the small size of the test groups and the large age difference between subjects. Errors may also have occurred in the analysis of torque and the electromyogram curve, and the data of some participants needed to be excluded due to issues with data quality. In summary, force production in the GM muscle is weaker in children with CP, but their muscle activation is distributed over a slightly larger area in the muscle. Despite the hypothesis, our results displayed hardly any difference between the CP and TD groups in the control of force production, however these results are affected by some limitations. The control of force production in the GM muscle did not correlate with walking ability in our small and heterogenous CP group.
authors: Ilona Repo

title: Lower limb orthotics in cerebral palsy
abstract: Uvod: Cerebralna paraliza je neprogresivna nevrološka motnja, ki nastane kot posledica okvare osrednjega živčnega sistema v obdobju razvoja. Zanjo so značilne trajne motnje v nadzoru gibanja, koordinacije in telesne drže, ki lahko pomembno vplivajo na posameznikovo samostojnost in funkcionalnost v vsakdanjem življenju. Pri osebah s cerebralno paralizo so najpogosteje prizadeti spodnji udi, kjer se pojavlja spastičnost, zmanjšana stabilnost, slabša kontrola gibov in patološki vzorci hoje, ki lahko sčasoma vodijo v razvoj deformacij in drugih sekundarnih mišično-skeletnih sprememb. Pomemben del obravnave predstavlja ortotična oskrba, katere cilj je izboljšanje biomehanike gibanja, stabilizacija sklepov in preprečevanje napredovanja deformacij. Namen: Namen diplomskega dela je predstaviti ortotično obravnavo spodnjih udov pri osebah s cerebralno paralizo in prikazati vpliv različnih ortotičnih rešitev na biomehaniko hoje in funkcionalno mobilnost. Metode dela: V diplomskem delu je bila uporabljena deskriptivna metoda dela s pregledom domače in tuje znanstvene ter strokovne literature. Za iskanje literature smo uporabili bibliografske podatkovne baze: ScienceDirect, PubMed, ResearchGate, Journal of Prosthetics and Orthotics in Google Scholar. Rezultati: V pregled literature je bilo vključenih šest raziskav, ki so obravnavale uporabo ortoz za spodnje ude pri osebah s cerebralno paralizo. Analizirane raziskave poročajo o izboljšanju parametrov hoje, predvsem hitrosti hoje, dolžine koraka, stabilnosti in poravnave sklepov. Stopnja izboljšanja se je med raziskavami razlikovala glede na klinične značilnosti preiskovancev, vrsto uporabljene ortoze in cilje ortotične obravnave. Razprava in zaključek: Uporaba ortoz za spodnje ude pri osebah s cerebralno paralizo pomaga omiliti patološke gibalne vzorce in preprečuje dolgoročni razvoj deformacij. Z ustrezno ortotično oskrbo osebi omogočimo učinkovitejše gibanje, ki je bolj varno in energijsko učinkovito. Uspešnost zdravljenja je odvisna od individualnih značilnosti uporabnika, vrste patologije ter izbire ustrezne ortoze, njenih komponent in materialov. Za doseganje optimalnih rezultatov je potrebno dobro poznavanje biomehanike gibanja, klinične slike cerebralne paralize in principov delovanja ortotičnih pripomočkov.
